blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: The items of a reflective psychometric scale can be read as a proposal about a construct's structure. Language models make that proposal measurable by converting each item into an embedding, a list of numbers, similar for similar meanings. We introduce semanticfa, an R package for semantic factor analysis, which factors item-embedding similarities. It also interprets factors, flags redundant items, builds short forms, and screens new items. A worked example analyzes the 50-item International Personality Item Pool Big-Five Factor Markers, embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, and compares the results with a factor analysis of 874,434 respondents. Retention criteria tied between five and six factors, and the tie rule kept five. Three corresponded mainly to single domains, and two blended most Extraversion items with five Agreeableness items. Each factor's congruence with its best-matching human factor (1 = identical) ranged from .92 for Openness to .52 for Agreeableness. Item pairs more similar in meaning tended to be answered more alike (r = .46 with raw responses), but same-domain reverse-keyed opposites, answered oppositely, were about as similar as cross-domain pairs (.58 vs. .57). Sign-flipping reverse-keyed items' embeddings did not improve agreement with raw responses and worsened it with reverse-scored ones. With five factors, a 25-item short form matched the domains better than all 200 random five-per-domain sets, but parallel analysis kept only three. We propose semantic-behavioral coherence, the agreement between semantic and response structures, as a measurable property of a scale, given an embedding model. Semantic factor analysis complements, and does not replace, response-based factor analysis.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Much of what psychologists measure, from personality traits and
attitudes to symptoms of anxiety and depression, is measured through
language ( hommel-arslan-2025 ; kambeitz-etal-2025 ) . The instruments are scales: sets of short statements, called
items, that respondents rate for how well each one describes them, such
as “I am the life of the party.” for extraversion. Because the
attributes these scales target cannot be observed directly, psychologists
treat them as constructs. A construct is a theoretical attribute whose
standing is inferred from the pattern of people’s answers rather than
observed. The standard tool for studying that pattern is factor
analysis. It identifies clusters of items whose responses correlate more
strongly with one another than with the rest of the scale, and it treats
each cluster as the expression of one underlying dimension, called a
factor. Each item’s loading is a number that expresses how strongly the
item reflects a factor. A scale is considered well built when its items
load on the factors that correspond to the constructs they were written
to measure.

blocks.en:
Factor analysis is almost always run on responses. Before anyone answers
a scale, however, its items already exist as sentences, and what those
sentences mean shapes much of the structure that factor analysis later
finds in the answers. The structure of a scale, in this sense, is the
number of factors it has and which items load on each. Items that
describe similar behavior in similar words tend to be answered alike, in
part because a respondent who endorses one statement tends to endorse
another that says much the same thing ( arnulf-etal-2014 ; hommel-arslan-2025 ) . Semantic factor analysis (SFA) builds on that observation by estimating the structure of a scale
from its wording alone. The R package semanticfa ( yanitski-westbury-2026 ) implements SFA, from
the item texts to the interpreted factors.

blocks.en:
What makes the wording measurable is a kind of language model called a
sentence-embedding model. Trained on very large collections of text,
such a model learns to represent any sentence as a long list of numbers
(4,096 for the model used in this paper), which are the coordinates of a
point in a space with that many dimensions. That list is the sentence’s
embedding. Training arranges the space so that sentences with similar meanings end
up close together, whatever their exact wording ( reimers-gurevych-2019 ) . The
embeddings of “I am the life of the party.” and “I talk to a lot of
different people at parties.” therefore lie near each other, while the
embeddings of sentences on unrelated topics lie far apart. The
similarity of two items can then be expressed as the cosine similarity
of their embeddings. If each embedding is drawn as an arrow from the
origin of the space to its point, cosine similarity is the cosine of the
angle between the two arrows. It approaches 1 when two statements say
nearly the same thing and approaches 0 when their meanings are
unrelated. In practice, the embeddings from such models all share some similarity,
as the internal word representations of contextual language models
commonly do ( ethayarajh-2019 ) , so even unrelated statements score well above 0.
This point returns in the subsection on reverse-keyed items. Computing it for every pair of items yields a matrix with the
same form as the correlation matrix on which factor analysis normally
operates. SFA is factor analysis of that similarity matrix, so no
respondent is needed at any stage.

blocks.en:
The semanticfa package organizes the analysis into four stages: building
the similarity matrix from item embeddings, deciding how many factors it
supports, extracting the factors and computing their diagnostics, and
interpreting each factor by relating the embeddings of its items to the
embeddings of candidate construct names. Beyond these stages, the
package offers refinement tools that use a fitted model to flag
redundant items, propose shorter forms, and screen newly written items
before they are administered.

blocks.en:
SFA does not replace factor analysis of responses. It recovers a second
structure over the same items, the semantic structure, which is built
from what the items mean rather than from how people answer them. Where
the semantic structure and the structure found in responses agree, the
items that are similar in meaning are also the items that people answer
alike. Where the two diverge, the divergence identifies the items that
wording and responses group differently and can suggest why. We call the
degree of agreement between the two structures semantic–behavioral
coherence , because the structure found in responses reflects how people
behave when they answer the items. In the worked example, that
behavioral structure, which we also call the response structure, is the
factor structure of the human responses, and the Results call its
factors the human factors.

blocks.en:
The Introduction develops these ideas in six subsections. It begins with
the evidence that item wording predicts how people respond, and then
explains how language models turn the meaning of a sentence into
numbers, the step on which both that evidence and SFA depend. Once
embeddings have been explained, the third subsection considers what the
semantic structure of a scale represents and how it relates to the
structure found in responses. The fourth addresses the first practical
difficulty any user meets, which concerns items worded so that agreeing
with them indicates less of the construct, because how an analysis
handles these items changes its results. The last two subsections turn
from the method to its uses. The fifth describes what semantic structure
can do before any data are collected, and the sixth introduces the
package together with the worked example that the rest of the paper
follows.

blocks.en: 1.1 Item Wording Predicts How People Respond
blocks.zh: 1.1 文字预测如何应对

blocks.en:
This subsection reviews the evidence that a scale’s wording predicts how
people respond to it. The evidence runs from single pairs of items to
whole scales and then to its limits: how well wording predicts the
correlation between two items, how well grouping items by meaning
recovers a scale’s intended factors, and what the disagreements between
semantic and response-based results reveal.
blocks.zh:
本小节审查以下证据,即比额表的措辞如何预测
人们对此作出反应。 证据从单对物品到
全天平,然后达到极限: 措辞如何很好地预测
两个项目之间的关联性,按意义分组项目的情况如何
恢复比额表的预期因素,以及
语义学和反应学结果揭示.

blocks.en:
The wording of items predicts, in part, how responses to them correlate ( arnulf-etal-2014 ; arnulf-etal-2018 ; gefen-larsen-2017 ; hommel-arslan-2025 ; hussain-etal-2024 ; kambeitz-etal-2025 ; nimon-etal-2016 ; ravenda-etal-2025 ; schoenegger-etal-2025 ; wulff-mata-2025 ) ,
and in the strongest studies it predicts a substantial share ( arnulf-etal-2014 ; hommel-arslan-2025 ) .
For example, arnulf-etal-2014 measured the semantic similarity of
item pairs in organizational-behavior surveys with methods such as
latent semantic analysis. Latent semantic analysis is an early technique
that represents each word by the texts in which it occurs and then
reduces these representations to a few hundred dimensions ( landauer-dumais-1997 ) . Across three samples, semantic similarity explained 47% to 79% of the
variance in the correlations observed in responses (the in-sample R 2 R^{2} of
regressions over item pairs), and 68% to 87% once the scale each item
belonged to was also taken into account. arnulf-etal-2014 explained
the result with what they called the semantic theory of survey response,
which holds that the relations among survey items are largely determined
by the items’ semantic properties. The program of work that followed is
summarized in an editorial by arnulf-etal-2021 . The early methods in this program represented words rather than whole
sentences, and on one kind of scale they predicted almost nothing. Item
meaning predicted almost nothing about responses to a five-factor
personality inventory ( arnulf-etal-2014 ) , and a reanalysis of the
same data agreed ( arnulf-etal-2018 ) . The authors tentatively
attributed this to how personality inventories are written. They
suggested that the items of inventories such as the one they studied
sample a wide range of past behaviors, so the answers carry information
that the wording does not supply ( arnulf-etal-2018 ) .
The worked example in this paper also uses a five-factor personality
inventory, and the studies with sentence embeddings described below have
since recovered structure in such inventories. Separately, hommel-arslan-2025 trained a sentence-embedding model
to predict item correlations and tested it on new items in a preregistered
study. After adjustment for sampling
error, its predictions correlated r = .59 r=.59 with the observed
correlations between single items and r = .84 r=.84 with the correlations
between whole scales, so the model predicted how whole scales relate more
accurately than how single items relate. For the scale-level
predictions, the embeddings of items worded against the construct were
multiplied by − 1 -1 before the embeddings of each scale’s items were
averaged, which requires knowing in advance which items are worded that
way.

blocks.en:
Wording also predicts some properties of single items. In educational
testing, the difficulty of an item can be predicted in part from its text ( peters-etal-2025 ) . Difficulty is commonly measured either as the proportion
of people who answer the item correctly or as a corresponding parameter
of a statistical model of the responses. Item
discrimination refers to how sharply an item separates people who are
high on the construct from people who are low on it. In one large bank
of English language arts items, discrimination was harder to predict
from text alone ( han-etal-2025 ) , although language models
fine-tuned to answer the items as simulated respondents recovered it
better on the items of a Grade 6 English language arts assessment ( ormerod-2026 ) .

blocks.en:
A stronger version of the finding concerns whole factor structures.
Grouping items, or facets of items, by the similarity of their meaning,
whether by principal component analysis, factor analysis, or clustering,
largely recovers the factors that established scales were designed to
measure ( casella-etal-2024 ; guenole-etal-2025 ; kambeitz-etal-2025 ; milano-etal-2025a ) .
For one clinical scale, a proof of concept found the same factor
structure in the semantic similarities as in the response correlations ( ravenda-etal-2025 ) . guenole-etal-2025 formalized the approach as pseudo-factor
analysis , in which the matrix of cosine similarities between embeddings is
factor-analyzed as a correlation matrix would be. The embeddings
were those of the items, pooled over the items of each facet, or of each
facet’s items embedded together as one text. Analyzed at the level of their
facets, the five- and six-factor structures of two large
personality inventories from the International Personality Item Pool
(IPIP), the IPIP-NEO-300 and the IPIP version of the HEXACO-240, were
largely recovered, with the theoretically expected number of factors and
an oblique target rotation toward the theoretical structure. The
loadings themselves correlated substantially with those from responses
but were often not equivalent to them, with Tucker congruence often
below .85. milano-etal-2025a found the same pattern across four scales,
including a set of Big Five markers and the Depression Anxiety Stress
Scales. In each scale, more than 70% of a construct’s items, on average,
had their highest loading on the same principal component, and the
items’ semantic loadings correlated with the loadings estimated from
responses. The finding extends, in part, to clinical symptom scales ( kambeitz-etal-2025 ) . A cognitive-network analysis of the
Depression Anxiety Stress Scales found a related overlap: communities of
the items’ words overlapped with the factors found in responses more
than random allocations of the same words would ( stanghellini-etal-2024 ) .

The match is strong but not complete. Studies that compared semantic

to a matrix of cosine similarities between item embeddings, so that a
model can be evaluated before any data are collected. They fitted such
models both to the similarities among the items of a character-strengths
inventory and to the responses of 31,697 people. A confirmatory factor model specifies in
advance which items load on which factors and tests whether that
structure fits the data. The semantic similarities correlated only
moderately with the response correlations ( r = .67 r=.67 ). Every model that
fit the semantic matrix also fit the responses, but about half of the
models that the semantic matrix rejected fit the responses as well. In that study, then, a model that fit the semantic matrix also fit the
responses, whereas a model that failed to fit the semantic matrix often
fit the responses anyway. In one unpublished study of a single sample and nine dimensions from
four scales, the strength of the relation between wording and responses
also appeared to vary across dimensions ( zhang-qiu-2026 ) . kojima-etal-2026 extracted factors
from both embedding similarities and response correlations for 145
psychiatric symptom items in Japanese. Both analyses produced a general factor on which all the items loaded. This factor was nearly identical in the
two (congruence = .97 =.97 ), whereas the narrower factors diverged.
Congruence measures how similar the loadings of two factors are. A value of 1 means that the two factors have the same pattern of loadings.
Insomnia and physical symptoms, for example, formed one factor in the
responses but not in the wording, plausibly because they occur together
in people, perhaps through bodily or physiological causes, without being
described alike. Semantic analyses of personality items also find agreeableness and
extraversion items overlapping in meaning ( casella-etal-2024 ; milano-etal-2025a ) . One possible reason is that
items of both domains describe warmth and sociability. Both studies
note, however, that the two constructs are also associated in human
responses ( casella-etal-2024 ; milano-etal-2025a ) . Such divergences are
informative, because they can mark the places where the way a construct
is described differs from the way people experience it. For that reason, this paper presents SFA as a
complement to response data rather than a replacement.

blocks.en: 1.2 Language Models Turn Item Meaning Into Numbers
blocks.zh: 1.2 语言模型转换项目含义为数字

blocks.en:
This subsection explains how the meaning of a sentence is turned into
numbers, in four steps that build on one another: the distributional
hypothesis about meaning, the word vectors that first applied it, the
sentence embeddings that SFA uses, and the cosine similarity that
compares them.

blocks.en:
The underlying idea is old. wittgenstein-1953 held that,
for a large class of cases, “the meaning of a word is its use in the
language.” In the same years, linguists stated a related claim, now called the
distributional hypothesis. The hypothesis holds
that words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings
and, conversely, that words that differ more in meaning tend to occur in
more different contexts ( harris-1954 ; joos-1950 ) .

分布假说. 假设

反之,在意义上更不同的词往往出现在

blocks.en:
Computational models of meaning apply this idea by learning, for each
word, a vector of numbers from the contexts in which the word appears
across a large body of text. mikolov-etal-2013 trained a small
neural network to predict which words appear near each other and used
the network’s internal weights as the word vectors, whereas pennington-etal-2014 built vectors directly from counts of how
often each pair of words occurs near each other. In both kinds of space,
words with similar meanings receive similar vectors. Differences between vectors often capture relations between words as
well. For example, the vector
for king , minus the vector for man , plus the vector for woman , lies close to the vector for queen , because the
difference between king and man is roughly the same as the
difference between queen and woman ( mikolov-yih-zweig-2013 ) .

Although such spaces are built only from where words occur, distances

Similarities between word vectors predict how similar people judge two

between words of opposite meaning, such as small and large , and the order of the words along that line tracked
people’s ratings of everyday words on many, though not all, such
features. How closely the order tracked the ratings varied widely from
one combination of word category and feature to another.

blocks.en:
Scale items are sentences rather than single words, so their meaning
depends on how their words combine. Modern language models represent
this combination with the transformer architecture, in which the
representation of each word can draw on the other words in its sentence ( devlin-etal-2019 ; vaswani-etal-2017 ) . A simple way to obtain one vector per sentence is to average the
vectors of its words. Averaged in this way, the vectors from the
transformer model BERT agreed less with human judgments of sentence
similarity than averaged vectors from an older word-level method, GloVe ( reimers-gurevych-2019 ) . reimers-gurevych-2019 addressed the problem by training the
model on pairs of sentences, so that sentences with similar meanings
receive similar vectors. The sentence-embedding models described at
the start of the paper are likewise trained on pairs of texts, although
many differ from this model in architecture and training objective. Their output for a sentence is the embedding that SFA uses. The embeddings in
this paper come from one such model, Qwen3-Embedding-8B, which is built
on a Qwen3 large language model ( qwen-2025 ; zhang-etal-2025 ) .

SFA compares embeddings with the cosine similarity introduced at the
start of the paper. The embeddings of two items with similar meanings,
such as “I am the life of the party.” and “I talk to a lot of
different people at parties.”, point in similar directions and have a
high cosine similarity. The embeddings of items with less related
meanings point in more different directions and have a lower one.
Embedding every item and computing the cosine similarity of every pair
therefore turns the wording of a scale into a matrix that factor
analysis can use. What the factors of that matrix represent is the
question the next subsection takes up.

blocks.en: 1.3 A Scale Has Both a Semantic and a Behavioral Structure
blocks.zh: 1.3 天平既具有语义结构又具有行为结构

blocks.en:
The evidence reviewed so far shows that wording predicts responses, but
it does not say what the semantic structure of a scale is evidence of.
This subsection argues that the semantic structure is part of what
defines a construct, and that its agreement with the structure found in
responses is evidence about that construct. The argument has three
steps. First, a construct is defined by its relations to behavior and to
other constructs, so the relations among the meanings of its items are
part of what defines it. Second, a scale’s items are written
deliberately to sample the construct, so their meanings are a designed
proposal about its structure. Third, the same factor-analytic procedure
can be run on either the meanings or the responses, so the agreement
between the two results is evidence about the construct. This subsection then states what that agreement can and cannot show and closes with two
consequences of the argument, one for naming factors and one for a
current critique of rating scales.

blocks.en:
The first step concerns what a construct is. cronbach-meehl-1955 argued that a construct is defined not by any single operation or criterion but by
its place in a nomological network , the set of lawful relations that
connect a construct to behavior, to observations, to theory, and to
other constructs. Two psychological scales therefore measure the same
thing when they relate in the same way to the same behaviors,
observations, and other constructs. The same relational view holds for
word meaning, as the previous subsection showed. Distributional theory
defines the meaning of a word by the contexts in which it occurs, and
nomological theory defines the meaning of a construct by its lawful
relations, so a construct stands to its nomological network as a word
stands to its distribution. Scale items fall under both theories at
once, because each item is both a piece of language and an indicator of
a construct. Validity theory applies the relational definition to
test scores. What a score means is established in large part by its relations to other
measures ( cronbach-meehl-1955 ; messick-1995 ) . Convergent relations are those
with measures of the same construct made by independent methods, and discriminant relations are those with measures of different constructs ( campbell-fiske-1959 ) . messick-1995 distinguishes six aspects of validity, two of which bear on SFA. The content aspect concerns whether the items are relevant to, and
representative of, the construct’s domain, and the structural aspect
concerns whether the way the items are scored mirrors the structure of
that domain. SFA bears on the first and, in part, on the second, because it examines
what the items say and how their meanings group.

blocks.en:
The second step concerns how items are written. Scale developers do not
choose items at random. They write an initial pool that deliberately
covers every kind of content that might belong to the construct, and
they keep the items that perform best when the pool is tried out on
respondents ( clark-watson-2019 ) . The wording they choose has
consequences of its own. clark-watson-2019 note, for example,
that responses to an item containing almost any negative mood term will
partly reflect neuroticism, so the exact phrasing of an item can change
what it measures. A scale’s items are therefore a semantic proposal , a
deliberate attempt to set out in ordinary language what a construct
contains and how its parts relate, and SFA measures the structure of
that proposal. This view assumes a particular measurement model, which
states how a construct relates to the responses to its items. In a
reflective model, the construct causes the responses to its items, so
the items should correlate with one another and factor analysis is
appropriate. This expectation that the items of a construct correlate is
the dominant view in psychology ( bollen-lennox-1991 ) . In a formative model, by contrast, the
items jointly determine the construct and need not correlate at all ( bollen-lennox-1991 ) . SFA is designed for
reflective scales, which include most personality and attitude scales.
For formative item sets, the measurement model does not constrain how
responses correlate ( bollen-lennox-1991 ) , so agreement between the
semantic and response structures cannot be assumed, and weak agreement
need not be a sign that something is wrong.

blocks.en:
The third step is that one procedure recovers both structures. Factor
analysis starts from a matrix of associations between every pair of
items and finds the few dimensions that best account for it. When the
associations are correlations between responses, the result is the
scale’s behavioral structure. When the associations are similarities
between item meanings, the result is its semantic structure. Both uses
have roots in the beginnings of personality measurement. galton-1884 proposed measuring character by systematically recording what people do,
and he estimated that English has at least a thousand words that
describe character, observing that each has its own
shade of meaning while sharing much of it with others. Twenty years
later, spearman-1904 supplied the inference on which factor
analysis rests, that correlated measurements reflect a common underlying
factor. Later lexical studies, which goldberg-1990 reviews, joined the two lines by factoring people’s
ratings on sets of trait adjectives, and Goldberg showed, with the most
comprehensive pools of English trait adjectives, that this recovers the
Big Five. Because only the source of the matrix changes,
the rest of the factor-analytic toolkit carries over, with some tools
adapted to embeddings. This includes deciding how many factors to keep ( horn-1965 ; kaiser-1960 ) , rotating the factors to make them easier to interpret, and testing whether a hypothesized
structure reproduces the observed associations ( joreskog-1969 ) .
Rotation re-expresses a factor solution so that each item loads strongly
on as few factors as possible, without changing how well the solution
fits. A rotation is either orthogonal or oblique ( bernaards-jennrich-2005 ) . An orthogonal rotation, such as varimax ( kaiser-1958 ) , keeps the factors uncorrelated, and an oblique
rotation lets them correlate. Testing a hypothesized structure carries
over only in part. The structure can be fitted to a similarity matrix,
but many tests of its fit cannot be computed, because they require a
sample size, which a similarity matrix lacks ( suarez-alvarez-etal-2026 ) .

blocks.en:
The agreement between the two structures is the semantic–behavioral
coherence introduced at the start of the paper, and agreement and
disagreement each have a specific interpretation. When the two
structures agree, the items that are similar in meaning are also the
items that many people answer alike, so two very different kinds of
evidence group the items into the same factors. In the terms of cronbach-meehl-1955 , this match can be read as one of the lawful relations that make up the
construct’s nomological network. When the
two structures disagree, the disagreement identifies the items that
wording and responses group differently and raises the question of why.
A researcher can then examine three explanations: (1) the items may be
worded ambiguously, (2) people may respond to them for reasons their
wording does not state, or (3) the construct may be organized
differently in behavior than in language.

Coherence is evidence about a construct, not proof that it exists. borsboom-etal-2004 argue that a test is valid for an attribute
only if the attribute exists and causally produces the test’s outcomes.
They also reject the view, adopted in the first step above, that a
construct is defined by its nomological network. On their account, a match between a test’s relations and a theory
corroborates the theory, and a mismatch signals a problem, but the match
is not what makes the test valid. A close
semantic–behavioral match therefore supports, but cannot establish, the
claim that a scale measures what it was written to measure.

blocks.en:
Embeddings can also help with the step of factor analysis that has
depended most on the analyst’s judgment, naming the factors. lara-etal-1992 identified factor interpretation as a major
problem in factor analysis, because many rotated solutions fit the data
equally well and the analyst chooses among the meanings they suggest
without a formal check. They proposed stating a candidate meaning for each factor as a
hypothesis and testing whether it is compatible with the variables that
load on that factor, and they anticipated that automatic interpretation
of factors might become necessary for very large problems. SFA can run an analogous test,
because a candidate name for a factor, such as extraversion , can
be embedded in the same space as the items. The cosine similarity
between the embedding of the name and the embeddings of the items that
load on the factor then measures how well the name fits.

One recent critique of rating scales motivates studying their semantic
structure separately. uher-2025 argues that rating-scale data are people’s
judgments of verbal statements rather than measurements of the phenomena
the statements describe, and calls the confusion of the two psychology’s cardinal error . If this is right, much of the correlation among
ratings is fixed by what the statements mean before anyone answers them,
and the semantic structure of the items is a real object that can be
studied separately. Uher also argues that language-model methods cannot
by themselves show how responses relate to the phenomena they describe. SFA estimates that structure from the wording alone,
before any data exist, and comparing it with the structure found in
responses shows how closely the responses follow the wording. Every
analysis of this kind, however, has difficulty with items worded
against the construct, and the next subsection explains why.

blocks.en: 1.4 Embeddings Do Not Represent Reverse-Keyed Items as Opposites
blocks.zh: 1.4 嵌入不代表反眼项目为反对者

blocks.en:
Most scales mix two kinds of items. A forward-keyed item is worded so
that agreeing with it indicates more of the construct, as “I am the life
of the party.” does for extraversion. A reverse-keyed item is worded so
that agreeing with it indicates less of the construct, as “I don’t talk
a lot.” does. Before responses are analyzed, the answers to
reverse-keyed items are reversed, so that a high score always means more
of the construct. In the raw responses, the two kinds of items correlate
negatively, because people who agree with one tend to disagree with the
other. This subsection explains why embeddings miss that negative
relation and describes three families of solutions that have been
proposed.

blocks.en:
The cosine similarity between two sentence embeddings almost never falls
below zero. Sentence embeddings share many features of language use that
are common to nearly all sentences, and these shared features keep every
pair of embeddings pointing in broadly the same direction ( hommel-arslan-2025 ) . In one of their examples, a widely used
sentence-embedding model rated “I am the life of the party.” about as
similar to its opposite, “I keep in the background.” (cosine = .35 =.35 ),
as to the compatible “I make friends easily.” (cosine = .32 =.32 ).
Factoring such a matrix does not yet separate reverse-keyed items from their
forward-keyed opposites ( suarez-alvarez-etal-2026 ) , and the
missing negative correlations are a major obstacle to reproducing the
correlation patterns of human data ( hommel-arslan-2025 ; pellert-etal-2026 ) . A loosely related observation appears in an early attempt to formalize factor
interpretation. lara-etal-1992 noted that properties studied in
sociological domains cannot be tied exactly to continuous scales, so
their meanings “are not unequivocally distinguishable from their
opposites” (p. 14). Their remark concerns the blurred boundaries of such
concepts rather than how embeddings represent reverse-keyed items, so
the parallel is only an analogy.

The proposed solutions differ in where they get the negative sign. The
first family takes it from the scoring key, which records which items
are reverse-keyed. guenole-etal-2025 multiplied each
reverse-keyed item’s embedding by − 1 -1 before computing cosines, as an
embedding analogue of reversing a response. This requires knowing the
key in advance, and it also rests on an assumption that the embedding
space does not meet. Reversing a response keeps the item’s content and
inverts only the scale on which it is answered. Multiplying an embedding
by − 1 -1 instead flips every one of its numbers, including the many that
encode features all sentences share, so the result points away from the
item’s whole topic rather than toward its opposite claim. The space is not organized so that negating a sentence corresponds to
inverting its vector. guenole-etal-2025 applied the flip before
averaging the item embeddings into one embedding per facet. With
that design, sign-flipping raised factor recovery for the IPIP-NEO-300.
For the HEXACO, however, it recovered the factors less often than the
other encodings tested and consistently failed to recover the
Emotionality factor.

The second family needs no scoring key and works from the embeddings
alone. SQuID (Survey and Questionnaire Item Embeddings Differentials)
takes the sign from the other items in the scale. It subtracts the
average of all the item embeddings, called
the questionnaire embedding, from every item’s embedding ( pellert-etal-2026 ) . Because this removes what all the items
share, the similarities that remain can fall below zero. The authors of
the method computed these similarities as correlations, whereas the
package computes them as cosines. They evaluated the method mainly on a
questionnaire of human values, and they noted that questionnaires with
reverse-keyed items still require methodological refinement.
Mean-centering, a second correction that needs no scoring key, subtracts
each embedding’s own mean value from all of its entries. After this
centering, the cosine between two embeddings equals their Pearson
correlation ( pokropek-2026 ) , so a constant offset shared by all of
an embedding’s entries no longer adds to the similarity. On the
embeddings of the worked example this made no practical difference, and
mean-centering does not by itself give opposite items negative
similarities. It is nevertheless the package’s default,
for reasons given in the Method section.

blocks.en:
The third family takes the sign from a model trained to recognize when
two sentences contradict each other. Natural language inference (NLI) is
the task of judging whether one sentence entails, contradicts, or is
neutral toward another, where one sentence entails another when the
truth of the first implies the truth of the second. hommel-arslan-2025 retrained a sentence-embedding model on a
corpus of about 570,000 sentence pairs that people had labeled in this
way ( bowman-etal-2015 ) . Contradicting pairs were given negative
target similarities, so the model learned to place sentences that
contradict each other far apart. Their final model, which was also trained further on correlations
between survey items, still predicted positive correlations for more
item pairs than the response data showed, 67% against 59% ( hommel-arslan-2025 ) . A cross-encoder
trained for NLI departs from embeddings entirely, because it produces no
item vectors at all. Instead, it reads the two items of a pair together
and estimates two probabilities, that the first item entails the second
and that it contradicts the second. Subtracting the probability of
contradiction from the probability of entailment gives a similarity
between − 1 -1 and 1 that is negative when the two items assert opposite
things ( hommel-arslan-2025 , cf.) .

blocks.en: 1.5 Semantic Structure Can Guide Scale Development Before Any Data Are Collected
blocks.zh: 1.5 语义结构可指导规模发展 在收集到任何数据之前

blocks.en:
Because SFA needs no respondents, it can be used at the stage of scale
development where changes are cheapest, before any data are collected.
Response data are costly to gather and have also become easier to
corrupt. westwood-2025 built an autonomous software agent that
passed 99.8% of the attention checks used to screen online survey respondents. An analysis of item wording cannot be corrupted in this
way because it uses no respondents. This subsection describes four uses
of semantic structure before data collection: finding redundant items,
comparing a scale with existing scales, choosing the number of factors,
and building short forms.
blocks.zh:
由于SFA不需要答复,可以在规模阶段使用.
在收集任何数据之前,在最廉价的情况下进行发展。
收集答复数据的成本很高,而且更容易
腐败 Westwood-2025 建立了一个自动软件代理商,
通过99.8%的注意力检查来筛选在线调查的答卷人。 对项目措辞的分析不能因此损坏
因为它没有被调查者。 本小节介绍四种用途
数据收集前的语义结构:
比较比额表与现有比额表,选择因素数量,
和建立短表。

blocks.en:
First, semantic structure can find redundant items. Internal consistency is the degree to which a scale’s items correlate with one another, and two items that say nearly the same thing raise it without adding content ( christensen-etal-2023 ) . christensen-etal-2023 developed
Unique Variable Analysis to detect such pairs in response data, and the
same screen can be applied to a matrix of item similarities. Redundancy
has also been flagged directly from embeddings. In a preliminary study, huang-etal-2025 clustered item embeddings. The clusters kept
the gratitude items apart from the others, but they grouped the items of
one grit facet, perseverance of effort, with the conscientiousness items.
This grouping matches the strong correlation between grit and
conscientiousness found in responses ( crede-etal-2017 ) . Prompted chatbots given the same task
recovered the broad structure but not consistent finer structure.

唯一变量 分析在反应数据中检测这种对,以及
同一屏幕可应用于项目相似度矩阵。 裁员
也直接从嵌入中标记。 在初步研究中,Huang-etal-2025将嵌入物集群. 保留分组
除了其他的感谢项目之外,他们将以下项目归类为:
以勤奋为重 坚持不懈
此分组匹配 grit 和 Q
在答复中发现自觉性(2017 Crede-etal). 任务相同的启动聊天机

blocks.en:
Second, it can check whether scales with similar names measure similar
things. Psychology has many scales for overlapping constructs, built in
research traditions that use different words for the same concept and
the same word for different concepts. Borrowing a term from the philosophy of
science ( sankey-1998 ) , wulff-mata-2025 call the
resulting difficulty of comparing theories and findings taxonomic
incommensurability . The two naming practices behind it produce two
named errors. A jingle fallacy occurs when two scales share a label but
measure different things, and a jangle fallacy is the reverse error, in which two scales have different labels but measure the same thing ( larsen-bong-2016 ) .
Semantic similarity makes both errors detectable. A jingle appears as
two scales whose labels are similar but whose item content is dissimilar ( larsen-bong-2016 ; wulff-mata-2025 ; wulff-mata-2026 ) , whereas a
jangle appears as two scales whose labels are dissimilar but whose item
content is similar ( larsen-bong-2016 ; rosenbusch-etal-2020 ; wulff-mata-2025 ) . wulff-mata-2025 embedded 4,452 IPIP items, 459 scales, and 277
construct labels in one space and flagged 504 candidate
fallacies under a quantile-based criterion. They also
argue that automated screening of this kind should inform expert
judgment rather than replace it ( wulff-mata-2026 ) .

similarity matrices built from the embeddings of items measuring six
personality facets. They applied two of the most common traditional
rules, parallel analysis ( horn-1965 ) and the Kaiser rule ( kaiser-1960 ) , to the principal components of these matrices. Both
rules overestimated the number of dimensions and recovered it in none of
the 500 simulated item pools, whereas Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA)
recovered it in 43.4% of them. EGA treats the items as a
network and finds dimensions as communities of closely connected items ( golino-epskamp-2017 ) . Its recovery
became almost perfect once redundant and unstable items were removed ( garrido-etal-2025 ) . The items in that study were written by one

decision is how many of each embedding’s leading coordinates to keep.

weighting agreement with a known structure against an entropy-based
measure of fit ( golino-2026 ) .

blocks.en: 1.6 The R Package semanticfa Brings the Whole Workflow Together
blocks.zh: 1.6 R套件语义法将整个工作流程结合在一起

blocks.en:
The methods reviewed above are scattered across separate papers,
scripts, and software, and each covers only one step of the analysis.
For example, pellert-etal-2026 shared code that reproduces their
SQuID analyses, and hommel-arslan-2025 released a web
application that estimates item correlations from item texts.
Even a recent framework for evaluating text-based psychological
measures, which applies natural language processing to the texts people
write, mentioned factor analysis of text embeddings in place of
rating-scale responses only briefly, as a possible direction for future
work on text data rather than on scale items ( low-etal-preprint ) . The semanticfa package ( yanitski-westbury-2026 ) brings the whole workflow together in R ( rcoreteam-2025 ) . It uses the psych package for
factor analysis ( revelle-2026 ) and, optionally, the EGAnet package ( golino-christensen-2026 ) for network analyses such as EGA ( golino-epskamp-2017 ) ,
so its results can be examined with tools that researchers already use.
The package follows the four stages previewed at the start of the paper.

该套件沿用了论文开头预览的四个阶段.

blocks.en:
1. Similarity construction computes the similarity between
every pair of items, either as the cosine of their embeddings, raw or
after one of the corrections described in the subsection on
reverse-keyed items, or with the NLI cross-encoder, which uses no
embeddings. The package calls the four embedding-based rules encodings and the cross-encoder’s output the NLI matrix. 2. Retention decides how many factors to keep. It can apply five criteria, some of them adapted to embeddings,
including parallel analysis and EGA, and report their consensus, the
number of factors they choose most often, with a tie going to the
smaller number. 3. Extraction and diagnostics fits the factor model and reports
five diagnostics. Three of them are fit statistics, which describe how
well the fitted model accounts for the similarity matrix. An optional
test compares these three fit statistics with the values that random
embeddings would produce. 4. Interpretation computes how similar each item is to each
construct, represented by the average embedding of the construct’s items
or by the embedding of its name. It also places items on axes defined by
pairs of opposite words and compares the semantic structure with a
theoretical or response-based one.

The name semantic factor analysis has, to our knowledge, one
earlier, independent use. muller-2026 used it for an analysis that recovered much of the
Big Five structure from trait adjectives with word vectors, in which each adjective’s
vector was weighted by its mean response. SFA as defined here differs in
two ways, because it needs no responses at all and it applies to any
scale items rather than only to adjectives.

两种方式,因为它完全不需要任何反应,而且适用于任何
缩放项目,而不仅仅是形容词。

The Method and Results sections form a worked example. We apply every
stage and each refinement tool to the 50-item IPIP Big-Five Factor
Markers, embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, and then compare the results

the same items ( openpsychometrics-2018 ) . The Method describes the
materials, the embeddings, and the choices a user makes at each stage,
and the Results follow the analysis step by step, from the first call to
the package to the comparison with human data. The Discussion summarizes
what the example shows, gives recommendations for users, and states the
limits of the method.

blocks.en: 2.1 Materials
blocks.zh: 2.1 材料

blocks.en:
The worked example uses the 50-item IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers, the
IPIP’s sentence-format counterpart ( goldberg-etal-2006 ) of the
adjective factor markers of goldberg-1992 . The inventory has ten short, first-person items
for each of the five domains, such as “I am the life of the party.”
for Extraversion. The IPIP is a public-domain collection of personality
items ( goldberg-etal-2006 ) , so these items are free to use and
reproduce without permission. It measures the five-factor structure that goldberg-1990 recovered across nearly complete sets of English
trait adjectives and across different raters and procedures, which makes
it a good test case for a semantic method. The semantic solution can be
checked against a well-established structure, and the items are short,
concrete statements whose meaning a language model can plausibly
capture. The inventory ships with the package as data(big5) ,
which holds the item texts, the item codes (E1 to O50), precomputed item
embeddings (see Embeddings below), a scoring key of + 1 +1 for
forward-keyed and − 1 -1 for reverse-keyed items, and each item’s domain
label.

blocks.en: 2.2 Embeddings
blocks.zh: 2.2 嵌入装置

blocks.en:
The main analyses use precomputed item embeddings from
Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( qwen-2025 ; zhang-etal-2025 ) , a sentence-embedding model whose
embeddings have 4,096 dimensions. Each of the 50 item texts was embedded
once, offline. An item’s embedding was taken from the model’s internal
representation of the item’s final token (last-token pooling), no task
instruction was placed before the item text, and the model’s final step
rescaled each vector to unit length. The resulting 50 × 4,096 50\times 4{,}096 matrix is the embeddings element of data(big5) .

一次,离线。 从模型内部提取了一件嵌入物

blocks.en:
Two interpretation tools described below also need embeddings of words
that are not items. Comparing items with construct names needs the five
construct names ( extraversion , neuroticism , agreeableness , conscientiousness , openness ), and
semantic projection needs the four words that define its axes
( anxious , calm , solitary , sociable ). The vectors for these nine words were taken from a precomputed lexicon of
single-word embeddings made with the same Qwen3-Embedding-8B model, with
the same pooling and rescaling and stored at half precision. The three
candidate items checked with the refinement tools were embedded with the
same model in the same way as the items. Every vector the analyses
compare therefore comes from one model, and all of the comparisons use
cosines, which do not depend on vector length. These auxiliary vectors
are also part of the reproduction archive.

blocks.en:
Finally, one similarity matrix is not built from embeddings.
The function sfa_nli_matrix() scores all item pairs with cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base , an NLI cross-encoder. It is a
DeBERTa-v3 model ( he-etal-2023 ) trained on natural language
inference data such as the Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI)
corpus ( bowman-etal-2015 ) and the Multi-Genre Natural Language
Inference (MultiNLI) corpus ( williams-etal-2018 ) . Both corpora
consist of sentence pairs labeled for whether the first sentence entails
the second, contradicts it, or does neither. Unlike the embedding models above, which
encode each item on its own, the cross-encoder reads the two items of a
pair together and scores whether one entails or contradicts the other.
The scoring runs in Python, called from R through the reticulate package ( ushey-etal-2025 ) with the Python library sentence-transformers . It is
the only step of the worked example that needs network access, because
the cross-encoder is downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub on first use.

valid correlation matrix, sfa() prints a message when it

Technical Reference.

blocks.en:
Retention. The user decides how many factors to keep. Each
factor has an eigenvalue, which measures how much of the total variation
in the similarity matrix the factor accounts for. The function sfa_parallel() runs parallel analysis ( horn-1965 ) , which compares each eigenvalue
with a threshold computed from the corresponding eigenvalues of matrices
built from random data. By default the threshold is the 95th percentile
of the corresponding eigenvalues of 100 such matrices. Following horn-1965 , the function counts the leading eigenvalues that
exceed their thresholds and stops at the first that does not, so an
eigenvalue that exceeds its threshold after that point is not counted.
In SFA the random data are random embeddings
with the same number of items and dimensions as the real ones, so a
factor that passes this comparison accounts for more variation than
chance similarity among random vectors would produce.
The function sfa_nfactors() adds four more criteria and
reports their consensus, the number of factors they choose most often,
with ties going to the smaller number. When the user does not fix the
number of factors, sfa() uses parallel analysis.

blocks.en:
Extraction and diagnostics. The main function, sfa() ,
runs the whole
workflow in one call, from item text, embeddings, or a similarity
matrix. Through the psych package ( revelle-2026 ) , it extracts the
factors by minimum residual, a method that chooses the loadings so that
the similarities the factors reproduce differ as little as possible from
the observed ones. It then rotates them by oblimin, a rotation that
allows the factors to correlate, computed with the GPArotation package ( bernaards-jennrich-2005 ) . It reports five diagnostics, described
in Table 1 : the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of
sampling adequacy (KMO) ( kaiser-1970 ; kaiser-rice-1974 ) , the root
mean square residual (RMSR), the common part accounted for (CAF) of lorenzo-seva-etal-2011 , the total entropy fit index (TEFI) of golino-etal-2021 , and McDonald’s omega total for each factor,
computed from the factor’s loadings ( revelle-zinbarg-2009 ) . This is
a one-factor omega for each factor’s items, not the hierarchical omega,
which zinbarg-etal-2005 distinguished from omega total and
which revelle-zinbarg-2009 recommend for judging whether a test
measures one construct. The
KMO takes the normalized form of kaiser-rice-1974 , which runs
from 0 to 1, and the printout labels its value with their terms, such as marvelous for values of .90 or more. The TEFI is
the version of the index based on Von Neumann entropy. RMSR, CAF, and
TEFI are the fit statistics, because each describes how well the factor
solution fits the similarity matrix. The cutoff conventionally applied
to the RMSR, a standardized root mean square residual of about .08 or
below, was derived for confirmatory models of response data by hu-bentler-1999 , who recommended supplementing it with a second
fit index, because in their simulations it was most sensitive to
misspecified factor covariances and less sensitive than other indices
to misspecified loadings. Values produced
by chance can pass it, as pokropek-2026 showed for the standardized root mean square residual of confirmatory
models. The option calibrate = TRUE therefore compares the
three fit statistics with the values that the same model produces on
random embeddings.
The function as_psych() converts a fit into the format of the psych package,
so that the psych package’s own functions can be applied to the semantic
solution.

Interpretation. Four functions help the user understand what
each factor means. Two of them represent a construct by its centroid,
the average of the embeddings of the construct’s items, or by its name
embedding, the embedding of the construct’s name, such as extraversion .

the package calls anchoring. It computes the cosine similarity
between each item’s raw embedding and each construct, leaving the item
out of its own construct’s centroid, and flags items that are more
similar to another construct than to their own. • The function sfa_project() adapts the semantic
projection of grand-etal-2022 , scoring items by a cosine rather
than an inner product and rescaling the scores. It subtracts the embedding of one word from the
embedding of its opposite, such as anxious from calm , and
scores every item by the cosine between its embedding and that
difference vector. The scores are rescaled so that 0 marks the first
word and 1 the second. • The function sfa_congruence() measures how closely the semantic

solution from responses, or a correlation matrix. Its agreement metrics
are defined where the Results use them. • The function sfa_jinglejangle() adapts the

compares the similarity of their names with the similarity of their
items and flags pairs where the two differ by 0.20 or more. This single
threshold is the package’s own, whereas wulff-mata-2025 set
separate cutoffs for the two similarities from quantiles of their
distributions.

blocks.en:
A single script, reproduce.R , ran every analysis. Every random
step of the main analyses used the seed 42, set either by the script or
by the package function itself. Three steps used other seeds or none. The five further human
subsamples of the comparison-data check used the seeds 1 to 5, the
parallel-analysis check across model sizes used the seeds 1 to 10, and
psych’s parallel analysis of the human responses was not seeded. It
runs its simulations in parallel processes (two worker processes, the
default of R’s mclapply() , because the script does not set the mc.cores option), so their last digits can differ between runs
of the script. The script is meant to be run from
top to bottom. Its output transcript, saved by R CMD BATCH , supplies every
number in the Results. The excerpts shown there are copied from it,
reflowed to fit the page and with omissions marked. The script runs the steps in
the order in which they were built, so its transcript does not follow
the list below. The list follows the order in which the Results report
the steps.

blocks.en:
1. Fit the model. The function sfa() fit the model to the mean_centered_pearson similarity matrix of the 8B embeddings.
This encoding was chosen before any factor was interpreted, because it
needs no scoring key and produces a Pearson correlation matrix. Parallel analysis chose the number of factors, and that number, five,
was then fixed for every later step. RMSR, CAF, and TEFI were finally compared
with their values in fits to 100 sets of random embeddings of the same
size. 2. Compare the encodings. All four embedding encodings were
built from the same embedding matrix and compared by the range of their
similarities, and atomic and mean-centered Pearson were also compared
entry by entry. To see how each encoding treats reverse-keyed items, E1
was also compared with its reverse-keyed counterpart E2 and with E5,
which is keyed the same way as E1. 3. Choose the number of factors. Parallel analysis compared
each eigenvalue with the 95th percentile of the corresponding
eigenvalues from 100 sets of random embeddings. It counted the leading
eigenvalues that exceeded their thresholds and stopped at the first that
did not. Its verdict was set against the consensus of the five criteria
in sfa_nfactors() , the number they chose most often, with ties
going to the smaller number. Velicer’s
minimum average partial test ( velicer-1976 ) was also run but not
counted in the consensus. The function sfa_dimselect() then
chose how many leading coordinates of each embedding to keep, the depth.
It ran EGA on the first d d coordinates at 148 depths:
147 depths spaced 28 apart, from
3 to 4,091 leading coordinates, plus the full
embedding of 4,096 coordinates. At each depth, EGA estimated
the item network with the triangulated maximally filtered graph ( massara-etal-2016 ) and found its communities with the Walktrap
algorithm ( pons-latapy-2006 ) . Two quantities were computed at each
depth. The first was the normalized mutual information (NMI) between the
EGA communities and the theoretical domains, which is defined in the
Results. The second was the TEFI of the EGA solution. Each was rescaled across the
depths to run from 0 to 1, and the chosen depth maximized 0.70 × NMI − 0.30 × TEFI 0.70\times\mathrm{NMI}-0.30\times\mathrm{TEFI} on the rescaled values, so
agreement with the theoretical domains counted for more than entropy
fit (see the Technical Reference in the Supplementary Materials). The
Qwen3-Embedding models support embeddings of a chosen, shorter size ( zhang-etal-2025 ) . This support rests on Matryoshka representation
learning ( kusupati-etal-2022 ) , which trains the leading
coordinates of an embedding to work on their own, so keeping the first d d coordinates gives a usable shorter embedding. The depth search was a
separate analysis. The main fit used the full embedding, because sfa() keeps every coordinate unless its dim_select argument requests the search. 4. Choose an embedding model. The similarity matrix and the
retention criteria, with each function’s default settings, were
recomputed from the 0.6B and 4B embeddings, and the first eight
parallel-analysis thresholds were recorded for each model. To see how
far each verdict of parallel analysis depends on the random embeddings
drawn, parallel analysis was also repeated for each of the three models
with the seeds 1 to 10. To
measure how clearly each model separates the five domains, we computed a
point-biserial correlation over all 1,225 item pairs. A point-biserial
correlation is a Pearson correlation between a two-valued variable and a
continuous one. Here the two-valued variable records whether the two
items of a pair belong to the same domain, and the continuous variable is
their similarity, so the correlation is high when same-domain pairs are
consistently more similar than cross-domain pairs. Its uncertainty at
each size was described by the item-level bootstrap described below for
the item pairs, and the within- minus between-domain gap in similarity
was also computed for each domain separately. 5. Interpret the factors. Each item was compared by cosine
similarity with every construct centroid and every construct name. The items were also placed by an adaptation of the semantic projection
of grand-etal-2022 on two axes, anxious – calm and solitary – sociable , each defined by a single pair of words.
They were then mapped in two dimensions with the package’s default
settings, a perplexity of 16 for t t -distributed stochastic neighbor
embedding ( vandermaaten-hinton-2008 ) and 15 neighbors for uniform
manifold approximation and projection ( mcinnes-etal-2018 ) , and
compared with their theoretical assignment. Both maps used the seed 42,
with the other arguments of the Rtsne ( krijthe-2023 ) and uwot ( melville-2025 ) functions at their defaults. How well each map kept the
domains apart was summarized by the share of each item’s five nearest
neighbors in the map that came from its own domain. Agreement between the
factors and the theoretical domains was judged against 1,000 random
permutations of the domain labels. The five
10-item subscales were screened for jingle–jangle fallacies, with any
pair of subscales flagged when the similarity of their names and the
similarity of their items differed by 0.20 or more. This threshold is
the package’s default, a heuristic rather than a published criterion. 6. Refine the items. Redundant pairs were flagged by Unique
Variable Analysis, using its published cutoff of 0.25 on the weighted
topological overlap defined in the Results ( christensen-etal-2023 ) .
Because a similarity matrix has no respondents, the package estimates
the underlying network with a nominal sample size of 1,000, a fixed
convention described in the Technical Reference, and the number of
flagged pairs was also counted with nominal sizes of 500 and 2,000.
As a check, pairs were also flagged when their similarity in the fitted
matrix, which here matches the raw cosine, was 0.85 or higher, a
stricter cutoff than the package default of 0.80. A 25-item short form kept the five items per domain most similar to the
centroid of their domain’s other items, and it was refit with the same
encoding, with its number of factors chosen by the same parallel
analysis (100 random embeddings, seed 42). To see how much of its
agreement with the domains selection alone provides, the short form and
200 random sets of five items per domain were also fitted with
five factors and compared with the domains. Three newly written candidate
items were then checked against the fitted model. They were written to
illustrate the three verdicts the check can give: an item that fits one
construct cleanly, an item that cross-loads, and a near-duplicate of an
existing item. By the package’s rules, a candidate cross-loads when its
similarity to its best construct exceeds its similarity to the next by
less than 0.07, and it is a near-duplicate when its similarity to an
existing item reaches the cutoff, set here to 0.85 to match the pair
screen (the function’s default of 0.90 gives the same verdicts here). 7. Compare with human responses. The responses to the
18 reverse-keyed items were reverse-scored by replacing each
response x x with 6 − x 6-x , so that 1 became 5 and 5 became 1. The
correlation matrix of these reverse-scored responses was factored with psych::fa ( revelle-2026 ) , using minimum residual
extraction, oblimin rotation, and five factors fixed at the theoretical five-factor
structure ( goldberg-1990 ) . The correlation matrix of the raw responses, without reverse-scoring,
was kept for comparisons with encodings that ignore the scoring key, and
it is the comparison for the default encoding, because neither uses the
key. A
conventional parallel analysis ( horn-1965 ) of the reverse-scored
correlations, the common-factor version in psych::fa.parallel with that function’s default of 20 simulated data sets, was run for
comparison. It compares each common-factor eigenvalue of the responses
with the mean of the corresponding eigenvalues of random data. The Supplementary Materials add comparison-data profiles ( ruscio-roche-2012 ) of the responses and the embeddings, with their
settings. Semantic–behavioral coherence was measured at
three levels: the factors, the item pairs, and the comparison across
encodings. At the level of factors, each semantic factor was matched to
the human factor with which its loadings had the highest Tucker
congruence ( lorenzo-seva-tenberge-2006 ) , defined in the Results,
in absolute value, and the mean of these matched values is the mean
matched congruence. The absolute value was used because a factor whose
loadings are all multiplied by − 1 -1 fits the data equally well, so the
sign of a factor carries no meaning. At the level of item pairs, agreement was the Pearson correlation
between each similarity matrix and each human correlation matrix over
the 1,225 item pairs. For the default encoding, which ignores the
scoring key, the headline comparison is with the correlations among raw
responses. Its uncertainty was described by an item-level bootstrap,
which resampled the 50 items with replacement 1,000 times and recomputed
the correlation over the pairs of distinct items, and the 2.5th and
97.5th percentiles of the resampled values give a 95% percentile
interval. After seeing the scatterplot, we also described the shape of
the relation, which was not planned in advance. An ordinary least squares
regression of the similarity on the human correlation and its square,
both uncentered, measured the curvature. Mean similarity was computed
for the pairs whose human correlation was above .20, within .10 of zero,
and below − .20 -.20 , cutoffs chosen after the scatterplot was seen. The
similarities were also correlated with the absolute values of the human
correlations. Finally, the pairs were grouped into three kinds: two
items of the same domain with the same scoring key, two items of the
same domain with opposite scoring keys (an item and a reverse-keyed item
of its domain), and two items of different domains. The same item-level
bootstrap gave 95% intervals for the curvature, measured as the
quadratic minus the linear R 2 R^{2} , for the difference in mean
similarity between the first two kinds of pairs, and for the difference
between the second and third kinds. Across encodings, a five-factor model
was fit under every encoding and to the NLI matrix and scored on the same
agreement metrics (Table S1 in the Supplementary
Materials).

blocks.en:
Choose the number of factors. Parallel analysis compared
each eigenvalue with the 95th percentile of the corresponding
eigenvalues from 100 sets of random embeddings. It counted the leading
eigenvalues that exceeded their thresholds and stopped at the first that
did not. Its verdict was set against the consensus of the five criteria
in sfa_nfactors() , the number they chose most often, with ties
going to the smaller number. Velicer’s
minimum average partial test ( velicer-1976 ) was also run but not
counted in the consensus. The function sfa_dimselect() then
chose how many leading coordinates of each embedding to keep, the depth.
It ran EGA on the first d d coordinates at 148 depths:
147 depths spaced 28 apart, from
3 to 4,091 leading coordinates, plus the full
embedding of 4,096 coordinates. At each depth, EGA estimated
the item network with the triangulated maximally filtered graph ( massara-etal-2016 ) and found its communities with the Walktrap
algorithm ( pons-latapy-2006 ) . Two quantities were computed at each
depth. The first was the normalized mutual information (NMI) between the
EGA communities and the theoretical domains, which is defined in the
Results. The second was the TEFI of the EGA solution. Each was rescaled across the
depths to run from 0 to 1, and the chosen depth maximized 0.70 × NMI − 0.30 × TEFI 0.70\times\mathrm{NMI}-0.30\times\mathrm{TEFI} on the rescaled values, so
agreement with the theoretical domains counted for more than entropy
fit (see the Technical Reference in the Supplementary Materials). The
Qwen3-Embedding models support embeddings of a chosen, shorter size ( zhang-etal-2025 ) . This support rests on Matryoshka representation
learning ( kusupati-etal-2022 ) , which trains the leading
coordinates of an embedding to work on their own, so keeping the first d d coordinates gives a usable shorter embedding. The depth search was a
separate analysis. The main fit used the full embedding, because sfa() keeps every coordinate unless its dim_select argument requests the search.

recomputed from the 0.6B and 4B embeddings, and the first eight
parallel-analysis thresholds were recorded for each model. To see how
far each verdict of parallel analysis depends on the random embeddings
drawn, parallel analysis was also repeated for each of the three models
with the seeds 1 to 10. To
measure how clearly each model separates the five domains, we computed a
point-biserial correlation over all 1,225 item pairs. A point-biserial
correlation is a Pearson correlation between a two-valued variable and a
continuous one. Here the two-valued variable records whether the two
items of a pair belong to the same domain, and the continuous variable is
their similarity, so the correlation is high when same-domain pairs are
consistently more similar than cross-domain pairs. Its uncertainty at
each size was described by the item-level bootstrap described below for
the item pairs, and the within- minus between-domain gap in similarity
was also computed for each domain separately.

Interpret the factors. Each item was compared by cosine
similarity with every construct centroid and every construct name. The items were also placed by an adaptation of the semantic projection
of grand-etal-2022 on two axes, anxious – calm and solitary – sociable , each defined by a single pair of words.
They were then mapped in two dimensions with the package’s default
settings, a perplexity of 16 for t t -distributed stochastic neighbor
embedding ( vandermaaten-hinton-2008 ) and 15 neighbors for uniform
manifold approximation and projection ( mcinnes-etal-2018 ) , and
compared with their theoretical assignment. Both maps used the seed 42,
with the other arguments of the Rtsne ( krijthe-2023 ) and uwot ( melville-2025 ) functions at their defaults. How well each map kept the
domains apart was summarized by the share of each item’s five nearest
neighbors in the map that came from its own domain. Agreement between the
factors and the theoretical domains was judged against 1,000 random
permutations of the domain labels. The five
10-item subscales were screened for jingle–jangle fallacies, with any
pair of subscales flagged when the similarity of their names and the
similarity of their items differed by 0.20 or more. This threshold is

Because a similarity matrix has no respondents, the package estimates

convention described in the Technical Reference, and the number of
flagged pairs was also counted with nominal sizes of 500 and 2,000.
As a check, pairs were also flagged when their similarity in the fitted
matrix, which here matches the raw cosine, was 0.85 or higher, a
stricter cutoff than the package default of 0.80. A 25-item short form kept the five items per domain most similar to the
centroid of their domain’s other items, and it was refit with the same
encoding, with its number of factors chosen by the same parallel
analysis (100 random embeddings, seed 42). To see how much of its
agreement with the domains selection alone provides, the short form and
200 random sets of five items per domain were also fitted with
five factors and compared with the domains. Three newly written candidate
items were then checked against the fitted model. They were written to

construct cleanly, an item that cross-loads, and a near-duplicate of an

similarity to its best construct exceeds its similarity to the next by
less than 0.07, and it is a near-duplicate when its similarity to an

blocks.en:
Compare with human responses. The responses to the
18 reverse-keyed items were reverse-scored by replacing each
response x x with 6 − x 6-x , so that 1 became 5 and 5 became 1. The
correlation matrix of these reverse-scored responses was factored with psych::fa ( revelle-2026 ) , using minimum residual
extraction, oblimin rotation, and five factors fixed at the theoretical five-factor
structure ( goldberg-1990 ) . The correlation matrix of the raw responses, without reverse-scoring,
was kept for comparisons with encodings that ignore the scoring key, and
it is the comparison for the default encoding, because neither uses the
key. A
conventional parallel analysis ( horn-1965 ) of the reverse-scored
correlations, the common-factor version in psych::fa.parallel with that function’s default of 20 simulated data sets, was run for
comparison. It compares each common-factor eigenvalue of the responses
with the mean of the corresponding eigenvalues of random data. The Supplementary Materials add comparison-data profiles ( ruscio-roche-2012 ) of the responses and the embeddings, with their
settings. Semantic–behavioral coherence was measured at
three levels: the factors, the item pairs, and the comparison across
encodings. At the level of factors, each semantic factor was matched to
the human factor with which its loadings had the highest Tucker
congruence ( lorenzo-seva-tenberge-2006 ) , defined in the Results,
in absolute value, and the mean of these matched values is the mean
matched congruence. The absolute value was used because a factor whose
loadings are all multiplied by − 1 -1 fits the data equally well, so the
sign of a factor carries no meaning. At the level of item pairs, agreement was the Pearson correlation
between each similarity matrix and each human correlation matrix over
the 1,225 item pairs. For the default encoding, which ignores the
scoring key, the headline comparison is with the correlations among raw
responses. Its uncertainty was described by an item-level bootstrap,
which resampled the 50 items with replacement 1,000 times and recomputed
the correlation over the pairs of distinct items, and the 2.5th and
97.5th percentiles of the resampled values give a 95% percentile
interval. After seeing the scatterplot, we also described the shape of
the relation, which was not planned in advance. An ordinary least squares
regression of the similarity on the human correlation and its square,
both uncentered, measured the curvature. Mean similarity was computed
for the pairs whose human correlation was above .20, within .10 of zero,
and below − .20 -.20 , cutoffs chosen after the scatterplot was seen. The
similarities were also correlated with the absolute values of the human
correlations. Finally, the pairs were grouped into three kinds: two
items of the same domain with the same scoring key, two items of the
same domain with opposite scoring keys (an item and a reverse-keyed item
of its domain), and two items of different domains. The same item-level
bootstrap gave 95% intervals for the curvature, measured as the
quadratic minus the linear R 2 R^{2} , for the difference in mean
similarity between the first two kinds of pairs, and for the difference
between the second and third kinds. Across encodings, a five-factor model
was fit under every encoding and to the NLI matrix and scored on the same
agreement metrics (Table S1 in the Supplementary
Materials).

blocks.en: 3 Results
blocks.zh: 3 结果

blocks.en:
Applied to the 50 IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers, the workflow produced
three factors that corresponded mainly to Neuroticism,
Conscientiousness, and Openness. Most of the Extraversion items and
five of the Agreeableness items were divided between two
blended factors, which also took three items from other
domains, and four Agreeableness items joined the Neuroticism
factor (Table 2 ). The similarities that the workflow
produced correlated r = .46 r=.46 with the correlations among the raw
responses of 874,434 respondents. The Results
follow the analysis from beginning to end, in the order a user would run
it. The first step fits the model in a single call and reads its output.
The next three steps examine the choices on which this call depends: the
encoding, the number of factors, and the embedding model. The fifth and
sixth steps use the fitted model to interpret the factors and to refine
the items, and the last step compares the semantic structure with the
responses of 874,434 people.

blocks.en:
The package’s main function, sfa() , runs the whole workflow in
one call. It builds the similarity matrix, chooses the number of factors,
extracts and rotates the factors, and reports the five diagnostics. Each
of these steps is also available as its own function
( sfa_similarity() for the encoding, sfa_parallel() for
retention) and can be run separately, as the next three steps do to
examine the choices that the call depends on. Automatic retention chose
five factors, which we will fix as nfactors = 5 for the rest of
the analysis. The encoding method is set to the default mean-centered
Pearson (see Method). Because this encoding ignores the scoring key, the
warning confirms that the scoring column in big5_df is not
used.

blocks.en:
KMO was .971, which means that the correlations among the items are
large compared with the partial correlations that remain between pairs of
items once all other items are held constant, so the matrix is well
suited to factoring. RMSR was .032. This means that the five-factor
model reproduces the observed similarities with a small average error,
and by the cutoff conventionally applied to response data, a
standardized root mean square residual of about .08 or below ( hu-bentler-1999 ) , the value counts as good. The
comparison with random embeddings at the end of this subsection shows how
little that reading means for embeddings. TEFI was − 27.71 -27.71 . TEFI
has no conventional cutoff, so the value is read against other solutions
and against fits to random embeddings. CAF was .412. This means that
the similarities the five factors leave unexplained still share structure
that additional factors could capture, so five factors account for only
part of what the items have in common. The factor correlations ranged
from .40 to .69. These high values are consistent with the
positive component of similarity that every pair of items shares, whose
size the first eigenvalue in Choosing the Number of Factors shows.
Calling summary(fit) adds McDonald’s omega total for each
factor, a one-factor omega computed separately for each factor from its
loadings on two sets of items ( revelle-zinbarg-2009 ) :

blocks.en:
Table 2 assigns each item to the factor on which it
loads most strongly and cross-tabulates these assignments with the
items’ theoretical domains. Three factors each correspond mainly to one
domain. MR3 takes eight of the ten Neuroticism items,
together with four Agreeableness items such as “I feel others’
emotions.” (A29). MR1 takes ten of the ten
Conscientiousness items and a few items from other domains, and MR4
takes seven of the ten Openness items. The two remaining factors
are blended factors, which means that each mixes items from several
domains. Between them they take nine of the ten
Extraversion items, five of the ten Agreeableness items,
and three items from other domains. Their composition is
consistent with a grouping by topic and phrasing rather than by domain. MR5 gathers seven
forward-keyed items about sociability and warmth from both domains, such
as “I feel comfortable around people.” (E3) and “I make people feel
at ease.” (A30). MR2 gathers ten items, all of them
reverse-keyed, that describe the absence of a disposition, such as “I
am not really interested in others.” (A27), “I don’t talk a lot.”
(E2), and “I am not interested in abstract ideas.” (O44). These items come
from four domains, so the embeddings appear to group them by their
negated phrasing as well as by their topic (Figure 1 and
Table S2 ). Not every reverse-keyed item joined
this factor, however. The other eight of the inventory’s
18 reverse-keyed items load most on other factors, six
of them on MR1. Some of these counts rest on near ties, items whose
two largest loadings differ by less than .03 (Table 2 ).
A24 decides whether the Neuroticism factor takes four
Agreeableness items or one fewer, and N14 and O46 decide how many items
from other domains the blended factors take, so these counts could
change under a slightly different solution. An item’s communality is the share
of its variance that the five factors jointly reproduce. Communalities
ranged from .566 (A23, “I insult people.”) to
.905 (N16, “I get upset easily.”). This means that
the five factors reproduce more than half of the variance of even the
least well explained item. The loading of N16 on MR3
slightly exceeds 1, which an oblique solution permits.
