blocks.en:
Conventional cutoffs for fit statistics need not transfer to
embedding-derived matrices. In confirmatory models with word
embeddings, pokropek-2026 found that values produced by chance
often passed the cutoff for the standardized root mean square residual
in models with four to eight indicators, although less often as the
number of indicators grew. That
cutoff was derived from fits to simulated samples of respondents of
several sizes ( hu-bentler-1999 ) , so it was set with the sampling
error of response correlations in mind, that is, with how much a
correlation varies from one sample of respondents to the next. An
embedding similarity matrix has no respondents. Adding calibrate = TRUE to the call compares RMSR, CAF, and TEFI with
their values in 100 fits to random embeddings of the same size.
The random embeddings are random vectors of unit length, and the cosine
similarities among them are close to zero. These cosines are computed
without centering the random vectors, whatever encoding the real fit
used, whereas the default encoding of the observed fit centers each
embedding. These random fits passed the
conventional RMSR cutoff easily, with RMSR between .0119 and
.0134, because a matrix of near-zero similarities leaves the
factors almost nothing to reproduce. Passing that cutoff therefore says
little about fit. For the same reason the observed RMSR (.032),
although higher than in every random fit, cannot be read as misfit,
because RMSR grows with the size of the similarities being reproduced.
TEFI behaves similarly. The observed value ( − 27.71 -27.71 ) was lower than in every random fit
( − 21.66 -21.66 to − 17.82 -17.82 , mean − 20.85 -20.85 ), so
none of the 100 random fits was as low, which shows only that the real items are
not random. The oblimin rotation did not converge in one of the
random fits, and over the 99 fits in which it converged TEFI
ranged from − 21.66 -21.66 to − 18.80 -18.80 . CAF has a different reference value.
Residuals with no shared structure give a CAF near .5, as the random fits
did (.501 to .532, mean .507, S ​ D = .003 SD=.003 ). The maximum came from the fit whose rotation did not
converge, and the other fits reached at most .512. The observed CAF (.412) was
lower than in all of the 100 random fits. This suggests that the similarities the
five factors leave unexplained still contain shared structure that random
embeddings lack, although, as for RMSR, a baseline of near-zero
similarities makes this a weak contrast. The Technical Reference in the Supplementary Materials
describes how the random fits are built and why they are a weak baseline.

blocks.en: 3.2 Choosing an Encoding

blocks.en:
There are several ways to turn item embeddings into the similarity
matrix that gets factored. The package implements four. The atomic encoding takes the cosine similarity between the raw embeddings.
The atomic_reversed encoding first multiplies each reverse-keyed item’s
embedding by − 1 -1 (here, 18 of the 50 items), then takes
cosines ( guenole-etal-2025 ) . The squid encoding (Survey and Questionnaire Item Embeddings
Differentials) subtracts the questionnaire embedding, the mean of all
the items’ embeddings, from every item’s embedding ( pellert-etal-2026 ) . The package then takes cosines, where the
original method correlated the results.
The mean_centered_pearson encoding, the package’s default,
subtracts each embedding’s own mean value from all of its entries. The
cosine of two such centered vectors is exactly their Pearson
correlation, so the similarity matrix is a correlation matrix. The function sfa_similarity() builds all four
from the same embedding matrix:

Supplementary Materials (Figure S2 ). Which encoding
best matches human responses is tested in the last step of the Results.

blocks.en: 3.3 Choosing the Number of Factors
blocks.zh: 3.3 选择因素的数目

blocks.en:
The five factors of the main fit were chosen by the retention step inside sfa() , and sfa_parallel() runs that step on its own.
With response data, parallel analysis compares each eigenvalue with
those of random data sets of the same size ( horn-1965 ) . SFA has no
respondents, so sfa_parallel() builds the comparison matrices
from random embeddings instead. It compares each eigenvalue with the
95th percentile of the corresponding eigenvalues from 100 such matrices.
It then counts the leading eigenvalues that exceed their thresholds and
stops at the first that does not (Horn’s sequential rule):
blocks.zh:
主要配位的五个因素由sfa()内部的留位步骤选择,sfa_平行()自行运行该步骤.
根据响应数据,平行分析将每个元值与
随机数据集中大小相同的数据(角-1965) SFA没有
答复者,所以 sfa_并行() 构建比较矩阵
从随机嵌入。 它将每个元值与
从100个这种基质中得出相应的基值的95%。
然后算出超过阈值的领先值和
在第一个不停止时(Horn的顺序规则) :

  Iterations: 100

Because parallel analysis is only one of several rules for this decision,
and the rules can disagree, sfa_nfactors() adds four more and
reports their consensus. The consensus is the number the criteria choose
most often, and a tie goes to the smaller number:

blocks.en:
1. The Kaiser rule ( kaiser in the printout) keeps every factor
whose eigenvalue is greater than one ( kaiser-1960 ) . 2. The empirical Kaiser criterion ( EKC ) compares each
eigenvalue with a reference value that depends on the eigenvalues before
it and on the ratio of the number of items to the sample size, and it
never lets that reference fall below one ( braeken-vanassen-2017 ) .
The criterion was derived for correlation matrices of sample data, so
the package puts the embedding dimension in place of the sample size. 3. The TEFI criterion fits solutions with one to 15 factors and keeps
the number of factors whose solution has the lowest TEFI. The package
uses the Von Neumann entropy version of the index ( golino-etal-2021 ) . Its authors developed the index to compare
candidate structures for response data, so its use on a similarity
matrix goes beyond the settings they tested. 4. EGA ( golino-epskamp-2017 ) keeps the number of communities of
closely connected items that it finds in the item network. The benchmark of garrido-etal-2025 used personality items written by a language model (GPT-4o) and a single
embedding model. In that benchmark, EGA recovered the dimensionality of
the embedding matrices more accurately than parallel analysis and the
Kaiser rule, both applied with principal component extraction.

blocks.en:
Parallel analysis and EGA indicated five factors, the Kaiser rule
six, the empirical Kaiser criterion six, and TEFI
two. Five and six were therefore each chosen by two criteria,
and the tie rule makes the consensus five, which matches the
number of domains the inventory was written to measure. The Kaiser rule
and the empirical Kaiser criterion agree here for a mechanical reason. Once the large first
eigenvalue is set aside, the empirical Kaiser criterion’s reference
values fall below one and are raised to one, so for this matrix the two
criteria amount to a single vote. The first eigenvalue (29.63, or
59% of the total of 50) is far larger than all the others
(Figure 3 ). This means that one general component, the
similarity that every pair of items shares, accounts for most of the
total variation in the matrix. The eigenvalues after it decline
gradually. A scree plot is usually read by looking for an elbow, the
point after which the eigenvalues level off into a straight line ( cattell-1966 ) , and
because this plot has no sharp elbow it does not settle the number of
factors by itself. The decision therefore rests on the formal criteria
above.

blocks.en:
Embeddings raise one further question that response data do not: how
many of the 4,096 coordinates of each embedding are needed to recover
the structure. The number of leading coordinates kept is called the depth, and the
package’s printouts call the full size of the embedding the embedding
dimension. The function sfa_dimselect() , described in the
Technical Reference, rebuilds the similarity matrix from the first d d coordinates for a grid of depths d d and chooses the depth whose EGA
solution best balances agreement with the theoretical domains against
TEFI. The grid had 147 depths spaced 28 apart,
from 3 to 4,091 leading coordinates, plus the
full embedding of 4,096 coordinates. The function selected
roughly the first third of the coordinates (1,431 of
4,096), at which EGA found five communities. Their
agreement with the theoretical domains, measured by the normalized
mutual information (NMI), which runs from 0 for unrelated groupings to 1
for identical ones and is defined under Interpreting the Factors, was
.704, the maximum over the depths evaluated. Across depths NMI
ranged from .193 to .704.
Figure S1 in the Supplementary Materials shows NMI and
TEFI at every depth. NMI rose quickly over the first few hundred
coordinates, stayed high but jagged over a broad middle range, and
declined toward the full embedding, while TEFI changed sharply from one
depth to the next. The selected depth is therefore the highest point of
a noisy curve rather than a sharply defined optimum. At the full depth, EGA found five
communities (NMI = .454). These NMI values compare EGA
communities with the domains and are distinct from the NMI of the
five-factor fit reported under Interpreting the Factors. Because the
choice of depth already favors agreement with theory, this result is
consistent with the main fit rather than an independent confirmation of
it.

blocks.en: 3.4 Choosing an Embedding Model
blocks.zh: 3.4 选择嵌入模型

blocks.en:
The last choice the call depends on is the embedding model, and in
particular its size. To measure how much size matters, the same 50 items
were embedded with three sizes of one model family, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B,
4B, and 8B (see Method), and the mean-centered Pearson similarity matrix
was built from each. Figure 4 shows the three matrices
side by side with the items grouped by domain. At every size, items are
on average more similar to items of their own domain than to items of
other domains. In the figure, the Neuroticism block along the diagonal is
clearly visible at every size, whereas the blocks of the other domains
are faint. Two statistics measure the separation more precisely. The
point-biserial correlation between sharing a domain and a pair’s
similarity, computed over all 1,225 item pairs, was .398
for 0.6B, .458 for 4B, and .416 for 8B (item-level
bootstrap 95% intervals .286 to .515,
.372 to .548, and .316 to
.535), and the mean
similarity of pairs within a domain exceeded that of pairs between
domains by .077, .077, and .079. By
both statistics, the separation between domains was similar at the three
sizes and did not rise steadily with model size. The intervals
resample items rather than pairs, because the pairs share items, and
they overlap widely, so the three sizes cannot be told apart on this
statistic. Computed for each domain separately, the mean similarity of
the domain’s own pairs exceeded that of its pairs with other domains at
every size, and the excess was largest for Neuroticism
(.127, .104, and .131, against at
most .077 for any other domain), the domain whose block
stands out in the figure.

blocks.en:
What changed with size was the number of factors that some retention
criteria indicated, each from a single seeded run with the package’s
default settings.
Parallel analysis retained three factors for 0.6B and
four for 4B, while EGA retained six and
six, and the consensus across the five criteria was
six for 0.6B and six for 4B. For 0.6B,
the parallel-analysis verdict of three rested on a narrow
margin, because the fourth eigenvalue, 1.370, fell just
below its threshold of 1.372. Repeated with each of ten further
seeds, parallel analysis gave the same verdict in every run for each
model size (three for 0.6B, four for 4B, and
five for 8B), so the verdicts did not depend on the random
embeddings drawn. Under the 8B embeddings, parallel analysis and EGA both retained the
theoretical five, and the consensus was five. The
other criteria did not move toward five. Under the 8B embeddings the
Kaiser rule indicated six factors and the empirical Kaiser
criterion six, as at the smaller sizes, and TEFI indicated
two at every size, so the criteria still disagreed at 8B.
Within this family, then, the 8B model was the only one for which
parallel analysis and EGA both indicated the five theoretical factors,
even though the separation between domains changed little. Model size
and embedding dimension also vary together here (1,024, 2,560, and
4,096 dimensions), and the dimension enters both the random baseline of parallel analysis,
whose first threshold was 1.50, 1.31, and
1.23 at the three sizes, and the reference values of the
empirical Kaiser criterion. The
comparison is therefore descriptive and cannot separate size from
dimension. Agreement with the theory the inventory was written to
express was also the reason the 8B model was used for the main analysis.
That agreement concerned the number of factors, because only under the
8B embeddings did the retention criteria lead to five factors. When five
factors were extracted at every size, the 8B solution did not match the
domains best. The NMI between each item’s strongest factor and its
domain, a measure of agreement defined under Interpreting the Factors,
was highest for 4B (.693, against .497 for 0.6B
and .527 for 8B, Table S4 ).

blocks.en:
A second inventory, the Depression
Anxiety Stress Scales ( lovibond-lovibond-1995 ) , showed a clearer
effect of size (see Model Size With a Second Scale in the Supplementary
Materials). There, the gap between within-scale and between-scale
similarity rose from the 0.6B to the 8B model, although the paired 95%
interval of the increase, from − .001 -.001 to
.053, just included zero. The three-factor solution merged
two of the three scales under the 0.6B model but separated all three
under the 8B model. The NMI between each item’s strongest factor and its
scale rose with each larger model, from .412 to
.700 and .834, and the rise held for a second
0.6B solution described in the Supplementary Materials, whose NMI was
.665. For some scales, then, a larger model can give factors
that match the scales more closely, even though it did not for the Big
Five inventory. For users of
this model family, we therefore suggest the largest model their
computer’s memory allows. Both results rest on three
models of one family and two English inventories, so whether the
suggestion holds for other model families and inventories remains to be
tested. The package’s default for embedding new text
remains the 0.6B model, because it needs the least memory (see Method).
The Supplementary Materials apply one further retention method, the
comparison-data method, to the same three matrices and compare its
results with those for the human responses.

blocks.en: 3.5 Interpreting the Factors
blocks.zh: 3.5 因素的解释

blocks.en:
Once the factors are fitted, the next task is to understand what each
one means and whether each item sits with the construct it was written
for. The function sfa_anchor() adapts the approach of wulff-mata-2025 . It computes the cosine similarity between each
item’s raw embedding and every construct, represented by the construct’s
centroid or by the embedding of its name, and it leaves each item out of
its own construct’s centroid. The printout lists the eight items whose
similarity to their own construct is lowest and marks those that are
more similar to another construct:

blocks.en:
The function sfa_project() adapts the semantic projection of grand-etal-2022 . For each axis, it subtracts the embedding of the
low-pole word from the embedding of the high-pole word and scores each
item by the cosine between its embedding and that difference, rescaled so
that the low-pole word itself scores 0 and the high-pole word scores 1.
Scores are therefore relative to the two pole words and can fall outside
the range from 0 to 1. Each pole here is a single word, so the scores
also depend on which words are chosen. The four pole words were
embedded with the same 8B model as the items, and the reproduction
archive stores their vectors together with those of the five construct
names. The script loads these auxiliary vectors as aux , uses aux_vec() to look up the vector of one word, and passes the
pole vectors to sfa_project() as poles :

blocks.en:
The scores follow the item’s wording and ignore the scoring key.
Reverse-keyed N12 (“I am relaxed most of the time.”) lands nearest the
calm pole (.82), opposite the anxious pole that the
forward-keyed Neuroticism items fill. This sensitivity to wording
suggests a use in scale construction, which the example illustrates but
does not test. Because the researcher
chooses the two words that define each axis, projection could show, before
anyone responds, whether an item pool covers both ends of its target
dimension, which items sit near the neutral middle, and how items from
different domains are ordered along a shared axis. The example did not
check whether an axis tracks its intended dimension or whether other
pole words would order the items in the same way. On the sociability
axis, the top five items include three Extraversion items about being
with and talking to people (E3, E7, and E5) and two Agreeableness items
about other people (A22 and A30). This mixing of the two domains at the sociable end is consistent with
the blending of Agreeableness and Extraversion in the factor solution,
although it rests on one axis and five items.

of four methods: t t -distributed stochastic neighbor embedding ( t t -SNE) ( vandermaaten-hinton-2008 ) computed with the Rtsne package ( krijthe-2023 ) , uniform manifold approximation and projection
(UMAP) ( mcinnes-etal-2018 ) computed with the uwot package ( melville-2025 ) , principal component analysis (PCA), or classical
multidimensional scaling (MDS). The following lines draw all four maps

blocks.en:
Most Neuroticism items are set apart from the other domains in the two
nonlinear maps (Figure 5 ), although a few, such as N12
in the t t -SNE map, lie among the items of other domains. In the two
linear maps they form a band along the second axis, with a few inside
the main cluster. The two nonlinear maps in the top row
emphasize local neighborhoods, so items with similar embeddings tend to
appear next to each other. In them, the Conscientiousness
items occupy their own region, as do most Openness items, and the
Extraversion items form a group. Several Agreeableness items lie next to
that group, and the rest are spread across the map rather than forming a
group of their own. The two linear maps in the bottom row preserve the
overall distances between items instead. The first two principal
components, the axes of the PCA map, account for 9% and
9% of the variance of the embeddings. Classical MDS on Euclidean
distances gives the same configuration as PCA up to reflection, so the
two panels are mirror images of one map rather than two separate views.
In that map the items of the four domains other than Neuroticism
overlap. The maps thus show, in two dimensions, a
blending of Agreeableness and Extraversion similar to the one in the
two blended factors of the semantic solution, MR2 and MR5
(Table 2 ).
The axes of the t t -SNE and UMAP maps have no interpretable scale, and
nonlinear maps can distort larger distances. mcinnes-etal-2018 also advise care with UMAP for data sets of fewer than 500 points,
because its approximations can then give suboptimal maps, and they note
that it can find apparent structure in noise. The t t -SNE and UMAP maps
are therefore for visual inspection only.
The share of each item’s five nearest neighbors that came from its own
domain, averaged over the 50 items, puts these impressions in numbers.
It was .72 in the t t -SNE map, .68 in the
UMAP map, and .42 in the linear map, against
.18 expected by chance, because nine of the other 49
items share an item’s domain. The nonlinear maps are built to keep
each item’s nearest neighbors near it, so their higher shares partly
reflect that design. In the linear map the Neuroticism items had the
highest share of any domain, .70, against .80
and .78 in the t t -SNE and UMAP maps.

blocks.en:
The function sfa_congruence() measures how closely the semantic factors
reproduce the theoretical assignment of items to the Big Five. It reports
two agreement metrics here, after assigning each item to the factor on
which its absolute loading is largest. The normalized mutual information
(NMI) is the information that two groupings share, divided by the
geometric mean of the entropies of the two groupings ( strehl-ghosh-2002 ) . The entropy of a grouping is the information
that the grouping carries on its own. NMI therefore runs from 0 (nothing
shared) to 1 (identical groupings). The adjusted Rand index
(ARI) is based on the proportion of item pairs that both groupings treat
the same way, either together or apart, corrected so that 0 means chance
agreement and 1 means identical grouping ( hubert-arabie-1985 ) . The
call compares the semantic factors with the theoretical domains:

The function sfa_jinglejangle() checks whether scales with similar names have
similar content ( wulff-mata-2025 ; wulff-mata-2026 ) . It represents each scale by two vectors, the average of its raw item
embeddings and the embedding of its name, and for every pair of scales it compares the
cosine between their item averages with the cosine between their names.
A pair is flagged when the two cosines differ by 0.20 or more. Here the
five 10-item subscales were treated as separate scales. In the call, sub_items holds the items of each subscale, sub_emb their 8B embeddings, and jj_lab_emb the 8B embeddings of the
five construct names:

No pair of subscales was flagged, which means that for every pair the
similarity of the construct names and the similarity of the items differed
by less than 0.20. The largest divergence, .17, was for
Agreeableness and Extraversion, the two domains whose items the factor
solution blended. Their item averages had a cosine of .89,
but the divergence still fell short of the threshold. Because the raw cosines between these
embeddings are all strongly positive, both similarities lie near the top
of their range, which makes a divergence of 0.20 hard to reach. A null
result on five subscales of one inventory therefore says little about
how sensitive the screen is. We see the tool’s main use in comparing
scales, including scales from different instruments, where mismatches
between labels and content can arise ( wulff-mata-2025 ) .

blocks.en:
Three functions refine a scale before any respondent is recruited.
The function sfa_redundancy() detects redundant item pairs with Unique
Variable Analysis ( christensen-etal-2023 ) . It first builds a
network from the similarity matrix in which each pair of items is linked
by its partial correlation, the association between the two items that
remains after all other items are accounted for, and in which weak links
are set to zero. It then computes the weighted topological overlap (wTO)
of every pair:
blocks.zh:
三项职能在征聘任何应答者之前都改进了比额表。
函数 sfa_redundancy () 检测带有独特特性的冗余项目配对
变量分析(Christensen-etal-2023). 它首先建立一个
网络来自将每对项目连接起来的相似性矩阵
由于其部分关联,两个项目之间的联系
在所有其他项目入账后保留,其中链接薄弱
设置为零。 然后计算加权地形重叠(wTO)
每对中:

blocks.en:
The printout lists the pairs from the largest overlap to the smallest
but keeps the row numbers they had before sorting. Each flagged pair
consists of two items whose relations to the rest of the scale overlap
strongly. The overlap column is the pair’s wTO, the degree to which the two items’
connections, including their direct link and their links to the other 48
items in the network, coincide, running from 0 (no shared pattern) to 1
(identical patterns). Pairs at or above 0.25, the cutoff of Unique Variable
Analysis, are flagged. The top pair, A24 (“I sympathize with others’
feelings.”) with A29 (“I feel others’ emotions.”), overlaps at
.462. This means that the two items relate to the rest of the scale
in similar ways in their wording, so either one is a candidate to drop.
Other pairs near the top of the list are also near-paraphrases, such as
N17 (“I change my mood a lot.”) and N18 (“I have frequent mood
swings.”), and O45 (“I have excellent ideas.”) and O50 (“I am full of
ideas.”). Every one of the eleven flagged pairs, including O42 with O44,
which the first printout leaves out, joins items from one domain, so the redundancy is repetition inside domains rather
than confusion between them. That pair is also the weakest flagged
pair and lies just above the cutoff, so the number of flagged pairs
depends on exactly where the cutoff falls. The number of flagged pairs
did not depend on the nominal sample size with which the network is estimated (see Method):
with 500 or 2,000 in place of 1,000, eleven pairs again
reached the cutoff. The flagged pairs form
ten redundant clusters, each a set of items linked by
flagged pairs, and the suggested-removals line names every item to drop
so that one item of each cluster remains, the one with the highest mean
absolute similarity to all the items. A simpler criterion, which flags any pair whose similarity in the fitted
matrix is 0.85 or higher (here matching the raw cosine), found
seven pairs in five clusters. Its top pairs
were N16 (“I get upset easily.”) with N19 (“I get irritated easily.”,
.938) and A24 (“I sympathize with others’ feelings.”) with A29
(“I feel others’ emotions.”, .933), and both of these pairs were also flagged by Unique Variable Analysis.
In all, five of the seven pairs that the
cosine criterion found were also flagged by Unique Variable Analysis.
Near-paraphrase pairs inflate internal consistency without
broadening content coverage ( christensen-etal-2023 ) .

blocks.en:
In the 25-item short form, the factors agreed more closely with the
theoretical domains, with NMI rising from .527 to
.810 and ARI from .402 to .571. This change
is descriptive, because it compares the five factors of the full form
with the three factors retained for the short form. Two further
comparisons, in which every item set was fitted with five factors, show
where the gain comes from. First, 200 random sets of five items per domain reached
a median NMI of .600 (95th percentile .734),
already above the full form’s .527, and a median ARI of
.367 (95th percentile .559), slightly below the
full form’s .402. Part of the gain in NMI therefore comes from
having fewer items per domain. Second, the short form itself, fitted
with five factors, reached NMI = .810 and ARI =
.707. Both values were higher than in any of the random sets (maximum NMI
.785, maximum ARI .656). This comparison with the random sets measures the
effect of selection, and it shows that selection by centrality improved
agreement with the domains beyond what a random choice of five items per
domain gives. Parallel analysis, which had given five factors for the full inventory,
kept only three factors for the short form, which means that
with five items per domain the similarities no longer cleared its
threshold for one factor per domain. Parallel analysis is a weak
criterion for embedding matrices (see the Technical Reference), so this
is one run of one criterion rather than a general verdict on the short
form. The table at the end of the excerpt assigns each item to the
factor on which it loads most strongly. Neuroticism kept a factor of its
own, while the Conscientiousness and Openness items shared one factor and
the Agreeableness and Extraversion items shared another. Because each of
these three factors holds whole domains, with every item on the same
factor as the rest of its domain, the three-factor NMI of
.810 is the value that any merge of two pairs of domains into
single factors gives. The items flagged as redundant were not removed
before the short form was built, and the short form kept both items of
four of the flagged pairs, A24 and A29 among them,
because its rule selects
central items rather than distinct ones. As the printed note warns, a semantic short form
is therefore a candidate for psychometric validation, not a finished
instrument.

blocks.en:
The function sfa_item_fit() extends the anchoring approach of wulff-mata-2025 to newly written items. It embeds each candidate and computes its cosine with the centroid of
every construct’s raw item embeddings. The report gives
the construct with the highest cosine, the margin over the next
construct, how the candidate’s cosine compares with the average cosine of
that construct’s existing items, and the most similar existing item. So
that the candidates are compared with the items in the same 8B space, the
reproduction archive stores their Qwen3-Embedding-8B vectors, generated
with the same settings as the item vectors. Before the call below, the
reproduction script places these vectors, and the archived 8B vectors of
the five construct names, in the package’s embedding cache, so the call
reads them from the cache instead of running the model. Without these
cache entries, the same call embeds the candidates and the construct
names with the model. The reference fit, fit_ns , is the main five-factor fit
rebuilt without the scoring column. Because the keying-free encoding
ignores that column, fit_ns is equivalent to the main fit, and sfa_item_fit() in any case uses only the item embeddings,
their theoretical domains, and the construct-name vectors:

blocks.en:
The three candidates, written to illustrate the three verdicts, received
the verdicts they were written for, which shows that the tool flags what
it was designed to flag rather than how often it is right. The first,
“I make friends easily.”, was more similar to the Extraversion centroid
than to the Agreeableness centroid by only .04, so it would not
distinguish the two domains. The second, “I am the life of every
party.”, had a cosine of .95 with E1 (“I am the life of the
party.”), above the 0.85 cutoff, which marks it as a near-duplicate of
an existing item. The third, “I finish what I start.”, fit Conscientiousness. Its
similarity to the Conscientiousness centroid was about as high as the
average for the domain’s existing items, it exceeded its similarity to
the next construct by .09, and no existing item was a
near-duplicate of it. A margin of this size falls in the band that the
printout labels some cross-loading risk , but it is above the
0.07 cutoff for a cross-loader, so the overall verdict is a clean fit.

responses from the Open-Source Psychometrics Project ( openpsychometrics-2018 ) , drop every row with a missing response
or a response outside the 1–5 range (keeping 874,434 of
1,015,341 response records), apply reverse scoring to the 18
reverse-keyed items ( 6 − x 6-x ), and run a conventional factor analysis:

blocks.en:
The warnings report that the noncentral chi-square probabilities, which
psych computes for its significance tests of fit, did not converge at
this sample size. They do not affect the loadings. Five factors were fixed at the theoretical five-factor structure ( goldberg-1990 ; goldberg-1992 ) . A conventional parallel analysis
of these correlations, computed with psych::fa.parallel() ,
suggested ten instead. This analysis compares each
common-factor eigenvalue with the mean of the corresponding eigenvalues
of random data of the same size, following horn-1965 but with
common-factor eigenvalues:

blocks.en:
Tucker’s congruence coefficient ( ϕ \phi ), which burt-1948 described for comparing two columns of coefficients and which later
became known by Tucker’s name ( lorenzo-seva-tenberge-2006 ) , measures how
similar the loading patterns of two factors are. It runs from − 1 -1 to 1, and values near 1
mean that the same items load on both factors in nearly the same
proportions ( lorenzo-seva-tenberge-2006 ) . By the benchmarks of lorenzo-seva-tenberge-2006 , values from .85 to .94 indicate fair
similarity, and values above .95 indicate good similarity, at which two
factors can be considered equal. The benchmarks rest on averaged ratings
by experienced factor analysts who compared loading patterns on 15 or 20
variables. The individual ratings varied widely and differed between the
two lengths. For pairs of low congruence they also differed between
research fields, with researchers in personality judging the factors to
be more different than researchers in intelligence did. The benchmarks
are therefore only approximate for the 50-item patterns compared here ( lorenzo-seva-tenberge-2006 ) . Each semantic factor matched a different human factor
(Table 3 ). The factor matched to Openness reached ϕ = .92 \phi=.92 , within the range of fair similarity, and the factors matched
to Conscientiousness and Neuroticism reached .84 and .80,
below it. The factors matched to Extraversion and Agreeableness
reached only .64 and .52. The semantic Extraversion factor
also matched human Agreeableness (.52) as closely as the semantic
Agreeableness factor did, which fits its mixture of sociability and
warmth items (Table 2 ). The mean matched congruence,
each semantic factor’s largest absolute congruence with any human factor
averaged over the five factors, was ϕ ¯ = .744 \bar{\phi}=.744 , the
average of three closer matches and two weak ones. The NMI and ARI
between the semantic and human groupings equal the values reported above
for the theoretical assignment (.527 and .402),
because every item’s largest human loading falls on its own domain’s
factor, so the human grouping is the theoretical one. These two metrics
therefore add nothing to that earlier comparison. The Frobenius similarity (.664) is the cosine between the two
solutions’ factor-correlation matrices, each written out as a single
list of numbers. It does not first match the factors, so its
value depends on the arbitrary order in which each solution lists them,
and it is not interpreted here.

blocks.en: 3.7.2 Encoding-Level Agreement
blocks.zh: 3.7.2 编码级协议

blocks.en:
Fitting a five-factor model under each of the four embedding encodings
and to the NLI matrix gives the comparison in Table S1 of the Supplementary Materials. Each is compared with the human
correlations that match it. The keying-free encodings and the NLI matrix
are compared with the correlations among raw responses. The
sign-flipping encoding applies the scoring key, so it is also compared
with the correlations of the reverse-scored responses, which apply the
same key. Sign-flipping left the grouping of the items unchanged (its NMI
and ARI equal those of atomic ). Against the raw responses, it
gave no gain ( r = .444 r=.444 for the flip, against .456 for
the default encoding). Against the reverse-scored responses, its
agreement was lower than that of atomic , which applies no flip
( r = .137 r=.137 , against r = .434 r=.434 ), and so was its mean
matched congruence with the human factors. A likely source of the drop in
both is the sign pattern that the flip imposes. Every unflipped
cosine is positive (the smallest is .394), so the flip makes
every similarity between a forward-keyed and a reverse-keyed item
negative, whereas reverse-scoring is meant to make the items of a domain
correlate positively whatever their keying.

blocks.en:
Against the raw responses, the NLI matrix agreed best ( r = .561 r=.561 ), followed by the squid encoding ( r = .490 r=.490 )
and by atomic and mean_centered_pearson ( r = .456 r=.456 ). The squid matrix is a poor basis for factor
analysis, however. Its KMO was only .022, which means that its
correlations are small compared with its partial correlations. The KMO
describes each matrix’s own factorability, and the three fit statistics
in the table (RMSR, CAF, and TEFI) describe how well each solution fits
its own matrix, so none of the four is comparable across the table’s
rows. The squid CAF near 1, for example, follows from its KMO
near 0. The NLI matrix matched the human loading patterns worst, with the
lowest mean matched congruence ( ϕ ¯ = .286 \bar{\phi}=.286 ). This
matrix had negative eigenvalues, however, which were raised to just above
zero before factoring, as the Supplementary Materials describe. Its
factor-based columns in the table (NMI, ARI, ϕ ¯ \bar{\phi} , KMO, TEFI,
RMSR, and CAF) therefore come from the repaired matrix, and its rankings
on them reflect the repair. Its r r with the raw responses uses the
original matrix and is the cleaner NLI result. These rankings are
descriptive, from a single analysis of 50 items, and carry no estimate
of their uncertainty. Gaps of a few hundredths between encodings, such as
those among the r r values above, cannot be distinguished without such
estimates, and even the larger lead of the NLI matrix on the raw
responses was not tested. The default mean-centered Pearson encoding
had the highest mean matched congruence ( ϕ ¯ = .744 \bar{\phi}=.744 , tied
with atomic ) and produced a matrix well suited to factor analysis
(KMO = .971). The table therefore does not single out one best
encoding, and it is consistent with the reasons the Method gives for the
default. On these embeddings the default and atomic gave the same
values to three decimals on every agreement metric, so the comparison
cannot separate them.

Across all 1,225 item pairs, the mean-centered Pearson similarities

responses are the right comparison here, because this encoding ignores

similar in meaning tended to be answered more alike, although meaning

1,225 pairs share 50 items, so they are not independent
observations. An item-level bootstrap, which resampled the 50 items,

blocks.en:
The worked example therefore gives the semantic–behavioral coherence
of this inventory, for this embedding model, a numerical value, a correlation of r = .46 r=.46 between semantic and human similarities across item pairs and a mean
matched congruence of ϕ ¯ = .744 \bar{\phi}=.744 across factors. The
coherence is uneven across domains. The Openness, Conscientiousness, and
Neuroticism factors resemble their human counterparts most closely,
whereas the Agreeableness and Extraversion factors resemble theirs only
partly. In the semantic solution, most of the Extraversion items and
five of the Agreeableness items were divided between two
blended factors, which also took three items from other
domains, and four Agreeableness items joined the Neuroticism
factor (Table 2 ). The composition of the two blended
factors is consistent with a grouping by topic and phrasing. One gathers forward-keyed items about
sociability and warmth from both domains, and the other gathers

blocks.en: 4 Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论

blocks.en:
In this example, with the 8B embeddings, the consensus of five
retention criteria, with ties going to the smaller number, matched the number of factors the
inventory’s authors intended, with two criteria choosing five
factors, two choosing six, and one choosing two. Three of the five domains corresponded mainly to single
factors. Where the semantic structure and the structure of the human responses
disagreed, the disagreement suggested where to look for a source. This
Discussion first summarizes what the example found and then explains
what the agreement between the semantic and response structures means,
because the recommendations, applications, and limits that follow depend
on what that agreement can and cannot show. It then draws
recommendations for users, describes where the package is most useful,
states the limits of the method, and ends with three directions for
further research.

blocks.en: 4.1 Summary of Findings
blocks.zh: 4.1 调查结果摘要

blocks.en:
This article introduced semanticfa , an R package that runs the
whole factor-analytic workflow on the similarities between the
embeddings of a scale’s items, and can also factor a similarity matrix
from an NLI cross-encoder, without any response data. The worked
example applied every stage and each refinement tool to the 50-item
IPIP Big-Five Factor Markers and compared the results with a factor
analysis of 874,434 people’s responses. It produced four main
findings.

发现。

domains. Three of the five factors corresponded mainly to one domain
each (Openness, Conscientiousness, and Neuroticism). Most of the Extraversion items and five of the
Agreeableness items were divided between the other two, which are

warmth, and the other gathered reverse-keyed items that describe the
absence of a disposition. The blended factors also took

(Table 2 ). Second,

against .57, a difference whose 95% interval included zero),

Third, two analysis choices changed the conclusions. The first was the
encoding. Sign-flipping the reverse-keyed items’ embeddings, the
apparent analogue of reverse-scoring, gave no gain in agreement with the
correlations among raw responses ( r = .444 r=.444 , against

without the flip). A likely source of that drop is the sign pattern that
the flip imposes on every pair of a forward-keyed and a reverse-keyed
item. The second was the reference
used to judge fit. By the cutoff conventionally applied to response

embeddings also passed that cutoff, so passing it says little about
embeddings. Fourth, the refinement tools proposed specific revisions to
the item pool. They flagged eleven redundant item pairs and
built a 25-item short form. Its agreement with the theoretical domains

ARI = .707, both above every random set, which is the effect of choosing the items closest to

one that nearly duplicated an existing item, and one that fit

blocks.en: 4.2 Theoretical Implications
blocks.zh: 4.2 理论影响

blocks.en:
The semantic and human analyses start from different data. The semantic
analysis factors the similarities between item embeddings and uses no
respondents, whereas the human analysis factors the correlations among
the answers of 874,434 people. The two agreed more closely for Openness, Conscientiousness, and
Neuroticism ( ϕ = .92 \phi=.92 , .84, and .80) than for the
other two domains. Because the two analyses use different information about the same
items, that agreement is evidence, for this inventory and embedding
model, that the items’ wording and people’s responses group the items of
these three domains in broadly similar ways, most closely for Openness,
the only domain in the approximate range of fair similarity. The embedding model may,
however, have learned the published domain assignment from listings of
the items in its training text, which would inflate the agreement and
cannot be excluded here (see Limitations). Such agreement can be counted
among the observable relations that make up a construct’s
nomological network ( cronbach-meehl-1955 ) . It is not proof that
the traits exist or cause the responses ( borsboom-etal-2004 ) .

blocks.en:
The disagreements are also informative, because they were concentrated
in two domains rather than spread across the inventory. In the semantic
solution, most of the Extraversion items and five of the
Agreeableness items were divided between two blended factors, which also
took three items from other domains, and four
Agreeableness items joined the Neuroticism factor
(Table 2 ), although a few of these counts rest on
near ties. The composition of the blended factors is consistent with a grouping by topic and phrasing rather than by domain. One gathered forward-keyed
items about sociability and warmth from both domains, and the other
gathered reverse-keyed items that describe the absence of a disposition,
from both domains and from Openness and Neuroticism. The semantic
Extraversion factor matched human Agreeableness (.52) as closely as
the semantic Agreeableness factor did (Table 3 ), which
fits this mixture. Two reasons are
plausible, although neither was tested here. English describes
sociability and warmth in overlapping words, and statements phrased as
the absence of something share the wording of negation across topics, whereas people’s reverse-scored answers keep the domains apart.
Other studies have found divergences of this kind and offered
plausible sources for them. Two studies found the same overlap of Agreeableness and Extraversion
items in embeddings and noted that the two domains are also associated
in human responses ( casella-etal-2024 ; milano-etal-2025a ) . The wording may
thus draw two related dimensions closer together than people’s answers
do, which is consistent with the mixture of warmth and sociability here,
where the human solution kept the two domains apart. The connotations of a word may also shift its
position in text away from the position that other measures give it. kmetty-etal-2021 , for example, found that health-care occupations
ranked lower in text than on a socioeconomic index of occupations,
plausibly because of their connotations of illness. People’s answers may
also share causes that the wording does not carry, as when insomnia and
physical symptoms formed one factor only in responses, plausibly because
they occur together in people, perhaps through bodily or physiological
causes, without being described alike ( kojima-etal-2026 ) .
A disagreement therefore points to the items and domains where these
possible sources can be investigated. How large the divergence is may also vary with the
construct. In one unpublished study of a single sample and nine
dimensions from four scales, wording appeared to predict correlations
least well in the dimensions whose items already correlated strongly,
by the authors’ reading of a random-effect correlation estimated across
those nine dimensions, in a model whose average effect of wording was
significant only narrowly ( p = .044 p=.044 ) ( zhang-qiu-2026 ) .

blocks.en:
Because coherence can be estimated, for a given embedding model,
theories of a construct can be asked to predict it, and those
predictions can be tested. If some clinical
constructs are networks of symptoms that cause one another ( borsboom-2008 ) , coherence should be lower for them than for
constructs whose symptoms share a common cause, because symptoms that
cause one another can correlate strongly in people’s answers without
resembling one another in meaning. The function sfa_congruence() makes that
prediction testable across instruments of both kinds. The same
reasoning yields predictions for two other cases. Formative indicators
jointly determine a construct and need not correlate ( bollen-lennox-1991 ) , so coherence cannot be assumed for them.
Method variance, the part of the correlations among responses that comes
from the method of measurement rather than from the content measured ( campbell-fiske-1959 ) , is a form of construct-irrelevant variance ( messick-1995 ) . We expect, although this was not tested,
that it also lowers coherence, because embeddings register the wording
of an item but not other features of the method, such as the response
format. Embeddings do register some features of wording beyond topic,
however, such as the negated phrasing that appears to have grouped
ten of the 18 reverse-keyed items here, so a method effect carried by the wording could instead
raise coherence. Studies of the
semantic theory of survey response suggest that the wording of a scale
can shape factor analyses of its ratings ( arnulf-etal-2014 ; arnulf-etal-2018 ) , but a factor analysis of
responses alone does not estimate how much of a scale’s structure comes
from its wording. Coherence indexes how closely the response structure
follows the wording. It is presumably related to that contribution of
the wording but is not the same thing, and the present data do not test
the relation.
Theories of a construct can be asked to predict this index.

blocks.en: 4.3 Recommendations for Users
blocks.zh: 4.3 对用户的建议

blocks.en:
The worked example suggests six practices for anyone running SFA. The
first five each follow from a specific finding, and the sixth follows
from the uneven agreement with human responses across domains. Where a
practice rests on the worked example, that evidence comes from one
inventory, one family of embedding models plus one NLI cross-encoder,
and English items, so each practice is a starting point that further
applications can revise.
blocks.zh:
实例表明,任何管理社会救济基金的人都有六种做法。 这个
前5个分别来自具体的调查结果,第6个
与人类在各个领域的反应不均匀。 哪个
实践取决于实例,即证据来自
存货,一个嵌入模型家族 加上一个NLI交叉编码器,
和英文项目,所以每个做法都是一个起点
应用程序可以修改。

blocks.en:
1. Use a keying-free encoding, and do not sign-flip
reverse-keyed items. Reverse-scoring a response keeps the item’s
content and inverts only the scale on which it is answered. Multiplying
an embedding by − 1 -1 , by contrast, reverses the sign of its cosine with
every item that is not also flipped, so the item becomes dissimilar even
to items on its own topic. In this inventory, sign-flipping gave no gain
in agreement with the correlations among raw responses ( r = .444 r=.444 , against .456 for the default encoding), and it
left the grouping of the items unchanged. Because the flip applies the
scoring key, its matched comparison is with the correlations among
reverse-scored responses, which apply the same key. On that comparison
it gave the worst agreement of the four embedding encodings, both over
item pairs and in loading patterns (Table S1 in the
Supplementary Materials). A likely source of the drop from the unflipped cosines is
the sign pattern that the flip imposes. After reverse-scoring, a forward-keyed
and a reverse-keyed item of the same domain correlate positively,
whereas the flip gives such pairs an average similarity of − .58 -.58 . In earlier work, which flipped item embeddings before
averaging them within each facet, sign-flipping raised factor recovery
for one inventory. For the HEXACO, however, it recovered the factors
less often than the other encodings tested and consistently failed to
recover the Emotionality factor ( guenole-etal-2025 ) . Embeddings from
general-purpose models do not represent reverse-keyed items as the
opposites of the forward-keyed items they contradict ( hommel-arslan-2025 ; suarez-alvarez-etal-2026 ) , raw embeddings rarely
give negative similarities between opposing items ( pellert-etal-2026 ) , and text methods older than embeddings could
not detect that an item is reversed either, so studies using them
corrected the signs of reverse-scored items by hand ( arnulf-etal-2018 ) and, for scales expected to relate negatively,
assigned negative signs from theory ( arnulf-etal-2014 ; arnulf-etal-2018 ) . In the worked
example, an item and a reverse-keyed item of its domain were on average

against .561). It also left a matrix poorly suited to factor analysis
(KMO = .022), so the default mean_centered_pearson encoding is the better choice for factor analysis. 2. Decide the number of factors from several criteria, and check
it against theory. The criteria disagreed here, with five and
six each chosen by two criteria and two chosen
by TEFI. In simulations with personality items written by a language
model (GPT-4o) and embedded with a single embedding model, the Kaiser
rule and parallel analysis chose too many factors more often than EGA ( garrido-etal-2025 ) , although here the adapted parallel analysis
agreed with EGA. The human analysis had a different problem. With
874,434 respondents, conventional parallel analysis endorsed
ten factors, possibly because with that many respondents
even very small factors exceed the mean random-data eigenvalues, although

blocks.en:
Use a keying-free encoding, and do not sign-flip
reverse-keyed items. Reverse-scoring a response keeps the item’s
content and inverts only the scale on which it is answered. Multiplying
an embedding by − 1 -1 , by contrast, reverses the sign of its cosine with
every item that is not also flipped, so the item becomes dissimilar even
to items on its own topic. In this inventory, sign-flipping gave no gain
in agreement with the correlations among raw responses ( r = .444 r=.444 , against .456 for the default encoding), and it
left the grouping of the items unchanged. Because the flip applies the
scoring key, its matched comparison is with the correlations among
reverse-scored responses, which apply the same key. On that comparison
it gave the worst agreement of the four embedding encodings, both over
item pairs and in loading patterns (Table S1 in the
Supplementary Materials). A likely source of the drop from the unflipped cosines is
the sign pattern that the flip imposes. After reverse-scoring, a forward-keyed
and a reverse-keyed item of the same domain correlate positively,
whereas the flip gives such pairs an average similarity of − .58 -.58 . In earlier work, which flipped item embeddings before
averaging them within each facet, sign-flipping raised factor recovery
for one inventory. For the HEXACO, however, it recovered the factors
less often than the other encodings tested and consistently failed to
recover the Emotionality factor ( guenole-etal-2025 ) . Embeddings from
general-purpose models do not represent reverse-keyed items as the
opposites of the forward-keyed items they contradict ( hommel-arslan-2025 ; suarez-alvarez-etal-2026 ) , raw embeddings rarely
give negative similarities between opposing items ( pellert-etal-2026 ) , and text methods older than embeddings could
not detect that an item is reversed either, so studies using them
corrected the signs of reverse-scored items by hand ( arnulf-etal-2018 ) and, for scales expected to relate negatively,
assigned negative signs from theory ( arnulf-etal-2014 ; arnulf-etal-2018 ) . In the worked
example, an item and a reverse-keyed item of its domain were on average
about as similar as two items from different domains (.58
against .57, a difference whose 95% interval included
zero), although people
answered them in opposite directions.
Three of the four embedding encodings use no scoring key: the unflipped cosines, SQuID,
and the default mean-centered Pearson encoding. SQuID agreed best with
the correlations among reverse-scored responses, but on the like-with-like
comparison with raw responses it fell below the NLI matrix (.490
against .561). It also left a matrix poorly suited to factor analysis
(KMO = .022), so the default mean_centered_pearson encoding is the better choice for factor analysis.

blocks.en:
The package is intended for the early stage of scale development that clark-watson-2019 call crucial, the writing of the item pool,
which comes before any data are collected. At that stage a researcher can screen a large pool of
candidate items, remove redundant ones early, and draft a short form,
all without collecting responses. The worked example flagged redundant
pairs, drafted a short form, and screened new candidate items. It
made no removal on the basis of the redundancy flags, however, and its
screen covered three candidate items rather than a large pool. Redundancy screening flagged eleven
redundant pairs, the strongest of them near-paraphrases, led by A24 (“I
sympathize with others’ feelings.”) and A29 (“I feel others’
emotions.”), whose wTO of .462 was the highest of any pair,
against a flag threshold of 0.25. Such pairs would be expected to raise
internal consistency without adding content ( christensen-etal-2023 ) ,
although the example did not check this in the responses. The short form
halved the inventory. Its agreement with the theoretical domains cannot
be compared directly with the full form’s, because parallel analysis
kept three factors for the short form. The rise in NMI from
.527 to .810 therefore compares a partition of the
items into five factors with one into three and is
descriptive only. The informative comparison is with random item sets.
200 random sets of five items per domain, fitted with five
factors, already reached a median NMI of .600, above the
full form’s .527, so part of the gain comes from having fewer
items per domain. Choosing the items closest to the center of their own
domain improved agreement further. Fitted the same way, the short form
reached an NMI of .810 and an ARI of .707, above
every random set on both (maxima .785 and
.656). The short form also kept both items of
four of the flagged redundant pairs, so building a short
form and screening for redundancy are separate steps. A short form
chosen for semantic centrality can also lose breadth that the construct
needs, in the same way that maximizing internal consistency can ( clark-watson-2019 ) . It is therefore a candidate for validation
rather than a finished instrument ( jung-seo-2025 ; wang-etal-2026 ) ,
and the package prints this caveat with every short form it builds.

blocks.en:
A second use arises when response data are scarce, unavailable, or
untrustworthy. muller-2026 recovered semantic structure, from
adjective vectors weighted by the mean responses of 55 people, in a
study where a confirmatory factor analysis of the same responses fit
poorly and merged two of its five factors, a failure that the author
attributed in large part to the small sample. The semantic analysis in
that study still used the
responses as weights, unlike SFA, so it is a precedent for semantic
structure helping where a small-sample analysis failed rather than for
response-free use. kambeitz-etal-2025 also note that collecting
the samples needed to develop a clinical questionnaire is costly and can
miss hard-to-reach groups, and that in some countries the cost can make
a sufficient validation sample infeasible. Synthetic
respondents that can pass attention checks ( westwood-2025 ) are a newer
threat to response data, and an analysis that uses no respondents cannot
be contaminated by them. The risk of mistaking machine output for human
data also applies to SFA itself, because structure derived from a
language model must never be reported as evidence about how people
respond. On a College Algebra test, none of six language models on its
own reproduced the distribution of human abilities, although an ensemble
of them approximated it better ( liu-etal-2025 ) . One framework that
simulates respondents also does not claim to replicate the psychological
processes by which people answer survey items ( lim-etal-2026 ) . For this
reason the package measures coherence with human data rather than
assuming it.

blocks.en:
A third use is comparing instruments. The jingle–jangle screen found nothing to flag in the Big-Five Factor
Markers. That null result from one inventory says little about the
screen’s sensitivity, because the two cosines it compares, between subscale item
averages and between construct names, were all strongly positive, so a
difference of 0.20 is hard to reach. We intend the screen mainly for
comparing scales, including those of different instruments, where
mismatches between labels and content can arise ( wulff-mata-2025 ; wulff-mata-2026 ) . The package
also complements item-generation tools such as AI-GENIE ( russell-lasalandra-etal-2026 ) . Such a tool writes new items and already removes redundant ones, and semanticfa could then apply a further screen for redundancy and
fit against the existing items before anyone answers them. This
combination was not tested here, and the worked example screened only
three candidate items written to illustrate the verdicts.

Finally, design choices affect what an analysis recovers, how private
and reproducible it is, and where it can run. Within this package, the
encoding and the size of the embedding model changed what the worked
example recovered (see the Results). Outside it, in a small preliminary
study of a different pipeline, clustering item embeddings recovered
structure that prompted chatbots did not recover consistently ( huang-etal-2025 ) . Open models that run on the researcher’s own
computer can also keep sensitive data private. hussain-etal-2024 make this point in their tutorial on
open-source language models for behavioral science. A model that is
saved and run locally, they note, keeps the data on the researcher’s own
hardware, where the model’s creators cannot access them. For SFA, recording the version of a
locally saved model has a further benefit, because every reanalysis then
uses the same measurement instrument. Once the item embeddings and the embeddings of any auxiliary words
exist, every step of the workflow described here that works from stored
embeddings runs without a network connection, provided Python with
NumPy ( harris-etal-2020 ) is installed for reading them. The semantic analysis is therefore designed

site and in a teaching laboratory, when both use the same embeddings,
seed, and software versions, including the linear-algebra library. Even
then, the layouts of the two nonlinear item maps in
Figure 5 can differ slightly between platforms (see the
Open Practices Statement). Across the package, only three steps call Python, namely
embedding new text, reading embeddings stored in NumPy files, and
building the NLI matrix, and embedding new text and building the NLI
matrix also download their models on first use.

blocks.en: 4.5 Limitations
blocks.zh: 4.5 限制

blocks.en:
The central limitation is built into the method, because SFA
characterizes the wording of items rather than the people who answer
them. Without respondents, it cannot show that a trait causes any
response, and it supplies none of the theory of how people arrive at their answers,
which borsboom-etal-2004 make the focus of validation research. Coherence must therefore never be reported as a validity
coefficient. Semantic evidence bears on two of the aspects of validity
that messick-1995 distinguishes. It addresses the content aspect,
which concerns which content a scale covers and how well, and it
addresses the structural aspect in part, because it
shows whether the meanings of a scale’s items group in the way its
scoring assumes. The remaining aspects require response and outcome
data. Close agreement between the two structures does not remove these
limits. kojima-etal-2026 found that factor scores from
responses predicted lifetime diagnoses better than scores that weighted
the responses by loadings derived from text, at least for the general
factor. SFA is best described, in the words that hommel-arslan-2025 use
for their own web application, as “a free pilot study of survey items”
(p. 15), and it should be followed by human data wherever they can be collected. schoenegger-etal-2025 also found that language models predicted
item correlations more accurately than most individual experts but did
not outperform the experts’ pooled judgment. Finally, in one study that
tested it, a finding that a model
fits the semantic matrix was more reliable than a finding that a model
does not fit. feraco-toffalini-2025 fitted a one-factor model to
each four-item scale of a character-strengths inventory. Every model
that fit the semantic matrix also fit the responses, whereas
about half of the models that the semantic matrix rejected fit the
responses as well.

blocks.en:
Coherence that is high would be consistent with part of the critique of uher-2025 , who argues that rating-scale data are people’s
judgments of verbal statements rather than measurements of what the
statements describe. Coherence estimates how closely the structure found
in rating-scale responses follows the meaning of the items, which is the part of that
critique that item text can test. Uher also argues that language-model
methods cannot by themselves show how responses relate to the phenomena
they describe, and SFA shares this limit. Studies of
the semantic theory of survey response estimated, with older text
methods, how closely item wording predicts the correlations among
responses, and those methods predicted almost nothing for a five-factor
personality inventory ( arnulf-etal-2014 ; arnulf-etal-2018 ) . Their
main estimates were in-sample proportions of variance explained,
computed on other instruments and samples, so they
are not directly comparable with the values found here. Here coherence
was r = .46 r=.46 at the level of item pairs, against the correlations
among raw responses, with a mean matched congruence of ϕ ¯ = .744 \bar{\phi}=.744 across factors, values for which no benchmark of coherence across instruments exists
yet. The theory of
meaning behind embeddings sets a further limit. Embeddings summarize how words are used in the language ( wittgenstein-1953 , §43) , not how an individual respondent reads
an item, so the part of each response that reflects one person’s
reading lies outside what SFA can measure. Coherence below 1 should therefore be expected even from a flawless
instrument, although how far below 1 is not known.

blocks.en:
A further limitation is specific to the inventory used here. The IPIP
Big-Five Factor Markers are reproduced on public websites together with
their domain labels, including in the documentation of the very data set
used as the benchmark here ( openpsychometrics-2018 ) . The embedding
model was initialized from a Qwen3 generative language model ( zhang-etal-2025 ) . That model was pretrained on about 36 trillion
tokens of text in 119 languages and dialects, which its technical report
describes only by broad domain, such as code, books, and multilingual
text ( yang-etal-2025 ) , so whether listings of this inventory were
part of that text cannot be checked. Generative language models can
memorize and reproduce text from their training
data ( carlini-etal-2021 ) , so the model may have learned which items
belong together from those listings rather than from what the sentences
mean, which would inflate the agreement between the semantic and response
structures. The semantic solution divided most of the Extraversion items
and five of the Agreeableness items between two blended
factors, which also took three items from other domains,
and four Agreeableness items joined the Neuroticism factor
(Table 2 ). This is not what one would expect if the
model had simply reproduced the published domain assignment, because
such a model would have kept the items of each domain together. Partial memorization of the
three domains that were recovered cannot be excluded without reworded
items, however, so coherence measured on well-known inventories may be an
upper bound. An important use of the package, checking new and
unpublished items, is the case that memorization is least likely to
help with. Re-embedding systematically reworded
versions of the items, with their meaning preserved, would bear on this
without new respondents and is left to future work.

blocks.en:
The random-embedding baselines have a limit of their own. Parallel
analysis and the fit calibration compare the observed matrix with
matrices built from random embeddings. Random vectors in thousands of
dimensions are nearly unrelated to one another, whereas real item embeddings are positively similar to one another, as
in the worked example and as representations from contextual language
models commonly are, a property called anisotropy ( ethayarajh-2019 ) . Every raw cosine in the worked example lay
between .394 and .938. Exceeding the random baseline is therefore a weak test for parallel
analysis. For TEFI, a value better than every random fit shows only that
the items are not random. The RMSR comparison is weak for the same
reason, and the CAF comparison should be read with the same caution,
because the baseline matrix is nearly an identity matrix. The Technical Reference in the
Supplementary Materials explains this problem and what a better baseline
would require. Until one exists, the number of factors is better treated
as a judgment informed by the consensus of several criteria and by
theory, as recommended above.

records with a missing or out-of-range response ( openpsychometrics-2018 ) , so its factor structure need not match
that of a representative sample. guenole-etal-2025 also note
that the people who wrote the text on which an embedding model was
trained may differ from the people who answer a scale, and that the more
the two populations differ, the less well the embeddings may stand in
for responses.

blocks.en:
The results also depend on the embedding model. The texts a model was trained on, how much context it reads, and how it
was built can all change which human behaviors its similarities predict,
and no model is best for every task, at least among word-level models ( mandera-etal-2017 ) . The embedding model is thus part of
the measurement instrument, so the stability of results across models
should be reported. The present results cannot show that stability,
because they rest on one model family (Qwen3-Embedding) and on English
items. Even a model’s full embedding need not be optimal, because preliminary
simulation evidence suggests that the signal can concentrate in a subset
of its coordinates ( golino-2026 ) . The
selected depth of 1,431 of 4,096 coordinates here, the
highest point of a noisy curve, is consistent with this but gives it
little support, because the depth criterion favors agreement with the
theoretical domains and so is not an independent test. In one study, embedding methods were also less accurate than expert
judges at assigning items phrased as behaviors, rather than as traits,
to their intended constructs, although on an inventory of concise trait
descriptions every model tested was more accurate than the judges ( milano-etal-2025b ) . In that study, the expert judges were
graduate students in psychology who, unlike the models, were given
definitions of the constructs, item length and instrument were
confounded with phrasing, and the authors note that
translating the behavioral items from Italian into English for some
models may have distorted their content. If the finding holds, the
structure of scales whose items describe behaviors may be recovered even
less accurately than the partial recovery obtained here for the Big-Five
Factor Markers, whose short first-person statements mix descriptions of
traits and of behaviors and were not classified by phrasing here. Clinical
experiences that are hard to put into words, and likely rare in training
texts, may be where semantic structure is least trustworthy ( kambeitz-etal-2025 ) .

blocks.en:
Finally, the refinement and screening tools carry their own caveats. Removing items
assumes a reflective model, in which the construct causes the responses
to every item. In a formative model, by contrast, each item is part of
the construct’s definition, so removing one usually changes the construct ( bollen-lennox-1991 ) . The cutoff that Unique Variable Analysis uses
was calibrated on simulated response data rather than on similarity
matrices ( christensen-etal-2023 ) , so how often it errs on
similarity matrices is unknown. Two items with nearly the same meaning
can still differ in how people respond to them, for example in how
readily people endorse them or how extreme their ratings are, so
similarity of meaning does not show that two items measure the construct
in the same way ( wang-etal-2026 ) . Every purely semantic verdict
about redundancy, including this package’s, should inform expert
judgment rather than replace it, and so should the screen for
jingle–jangle fallacies ( wulff-mata-2026 ) .

blocks.en: 4.6 Future Directions
blocks.zh: 4.6 未来方向

blocks.en:
Three directions follow from these results and their limits. The first
is comparative,
because no one can say what counts as high or low coherence until it
has been estimated across instruments, domains, and populations. The
worked example, which analyzed one carefully constructed inventory,
provides a single data point, and the largest differences may lie
between kinds of constructs. One prediction and two findings bear on this question, and each awaits
a systematic test with a common toolkit. If the symptoms of some clinical
constructs cause one another ( borsboom-2008 ) , those constructs
should show lower coherence than common-cause constructs, as argued
above. In one unpublished study, the strength of the relation between
meaning and correlation appeared to vary across nine dimensions from four
scales that measure different constructs ( zhang-qiu-2026 ) . milano-etal-2025b found that embedding methods were generally
less accurate than expert judges at assigning items phrased as behaviors to
their constructs. The judges were graduate students in psychology who, unlike
the models, were given definitions of the constructs, item length and
instrument were confounded with phrasing, and translating the behavioral
items into English for some models may have distorted their content. That finding
concerns how well the intended structure is recovered rather than
coherence, and the phrasing of items rather than the kind of construct.
If it holds, however, whether items are phrased as behaviors or as
traits, which varies across instruments, may also produce differences
in coherence between them.

blocks.en:
The second direction is methodological. It concerns four settings that
the present analysis fixed or examined only narrowly, and one test that
it left open. The analysis used a single model
family and compared only three sizes within it. Because results can depend
on the embedding model, as mandera-etal-2017 found among
word-level models, their stability across
model families should be reported the way agreement across raters is. The number of an embedding’s leading coordinates to use ( golino-2026 ) was examined here only with a criterion that favors
agreement with the theoretical domains, and the main fit used the full
embedding, which is the package’s default. The depth could be examined
in every analysis, with a criterion that does not depend on the
theoretical domains. The cutoffs for redundancy
screening should be recalibrated on similarity matrices instead of being
inherited from simulations of response data ( christensen-etal-2023 ) .
The random-embedding baselines could be computed once for common numbers
of items, embedding sizes, and encodings, and matched to the positive
similarity that real item embeddings share, so that a Monte Carlo reference of the kind pokropek-2026 used
would require looking up a table rather than running a new simulation.
A precomputed baseline would still leave open what it should hold fixed
from one draw to the next (see the Technical Reference). A particularly hard open problem among these is a
better baseline for deciding the number of factors, which the Technical
Reference discusses in detail. The test left open is the one for
memorization described in the Limitations. Re-embedding systematically
reworded versions of a published inventory, with the meaning of each
item preserved, and comparing their semantic structure with that of the
original wording and with the existing human responses would help show,
without new respondents, whether the agreement found here depends on the
model having seen the published items.

The third direction extends screening before data collection to
translated scales. In one study, a scale adapted from English into Polish with a generative
model performed at or near a human adaptation on most psychometric
criteria, with slightly lower reliability ( grobelny-etal-2025 ) , but without responses their structure cannot be
checked until the adapted scale has been administered. SFA could check
the adaptation’s semantic structure earlier by embedding the original and the adapted items in a shared
multilingual space. If the model represents the two languages
comparably, which would itself need to be tested, the agreement metrics
could indicate whether the wording of the adaptation has drifted from
the original semantic structure. The response structure of the adapted
scale would still have to be confirmed once it has been administered.

The first and third directions keep the division of labor that these
results suggest, in which the analysis of wording can be automated but its
verdicts remain hypotheses for response data to test. More
than thirty years ago, lara-etal-1992 proposed testing a
candidate meaning for each factor against the variables that load on it,
and anticipated that automatic semantic interpretation of factor
solutions might become necessary for very large problems. Sentence embeddings now make construct-level versions of such tests
computable, such as comparing items with construct names and centroids, and semanticfa implements semantic factor analysis as a standard factor-analytic
workflow in R. Three tasks still require response data
and expert judgment: explaining how people arrive at their answers,
relating scores to outcomes, and deciding when a well-characterized set
of items has become a validated measure.
