blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
A rating scale has two structures that factor analysis can examine: the
correlations among people’s responses and the organization of the
language that drew those responses. Methods for the first have been
developed for over a century ( spearman-1904 ) . Methods for the
second, which work from the meanings of the items, are recent. Most use
sentence-embedding models, such as Sentence-BERT ( reimers-gurevych-2019 ) , and their precursors represented words
rather than whole sentences ( arnulf-etal-2014 ) . As the Introduction
described, the published ones have been scattered across separate
papers, scripts, and software. The semanticfa package brings the stages of the factor-analytic
workflow together in one R package. It runs that workflow on the
similarities between item embeddings and can also factor the NLI matrix,
whose similarities come from a natural language inference cross-encoder
rather than from embeddings, although the steps that need embeddings,
such as the random-embedding baselines and the anchoring of items to
construct centroids, do not apply to it. The workflow covers a choice among
encodings, retention by several criteria, diagnostics with an optional
comparison of three fit statistics with fits to random embeddings, tools
for interpretation, and tools for refinement. The semantic analysis
itself needs no responses. Because it works from fixed, archived
embeddings, it is designed so that its numerical results can be
reproduced from those embeddings with the seeds given in the Method and
the software versions and linear-algebra library given in the Open
Practices Statement, apart from small platform
differences in the t t -SNE and UMAP layouts. The comparison with human
responses also needs the downloaded response file, and psych’s parallel
analysis of those responses is not seeded and runs in parallel
processes, so the last digits of its random-data eigenvalues can differ
between runs. The NLI matrix is a
further exception. It does not come from the archived embeddings, and the
cross-encoder that computes it is downloaded on first use. The Open
Practices Statement records the revision of the cross-encoder that was
used. On a well-understood
inventory embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, the consensus of five
retention criteria, with ties going to
the smaller number, was five factors, the number of
domains the inventory was written to measure, after two criteria chose
five, two chose six, and one chose two. With the two smaller models of
the same family, the consensus was six for 0.6B and
six for 4B. Three factors
corresponded mainly to single domains (Openness, Conscientiousness, and
Neuroticism). Most of the Extraversion items and five of
the Agreeableness items were divided between two blended factors, which
also took three items from other domains, and
four Agreeableness items joined the Neuroticism factor
(Table 2 ), although a few of these counts rest on near
ties. One blended factor gathered forward-keyed
items about sociability and warmth, and the other gathered reverse-keyed
items that describe the absence of a disposition. Agreement with the
factor structure of 874,434 respondents was closer for Openness,
Conscientiousness, and Neuroticism ( ϕ = .92 \phi=.92 , .84, and
.80, with only Openness in the range of fair similarity) and weaker
for Extraversion and Agreeableness. Two reasons are plausible, although
neither was tested here. English describes warmth and sociability in
overlapping words, and statements that describe the absence of a
disposition share the wording of negation across topics. For this
inventory and embedding model, sign-flipping the embeddings of
reverse-keyed items agreed less with reverse-scored human responses than
leaving them unflipped did. The package’s refinement tools, which need
no responses, flagged redundant item pairs, built a candidate short
form, and screened three new items written to illustrate its verdicts,
so revisions of this kind can be drafted before any data are collected,
as candidates to be validated once responses exist.
We propose that the agreement between the two structures,
semantic–behavioral coherence, be treated as a measurable property of a
scale, for a given embedding model, and counted among the relations in
the nomological network of the construct the scale measures. In the
worked example, coherence was summarized by the correlation across item
pairs between semantic similarities and the correlations among raw
responses ( r = .46 r=.46 ) and by the mean matched congruence of the
factors ( ϕ ¯ = .744 \bar{\phi}=.744 ). For a given embedding model,
high coherence is consistent with a scale’s wording and its respondents’
answers grouping the items in the same way, although what counts as high
remains to be established.
Low coherence points to the domains and items where the two part and
gives a starting point for asking why. For a given embedding model, SFA
estimates the structure that a scale’s wording implies before any
respondent is recruited, and once responses exist, coherence shows how
closely the structure of the responses agrees with that wording.

blocks.en:
A self-contained reproduction archive regenerates every number, table,
and figure in the worked example from raw inputs. It is kept in the reproduce folder of the package’s GitHub repository
( https://github.com/devon7y/semanticfa ), and the release that
accompanies this paper is archived on Zenodo
( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23696188 ). It contains the master script ( reproduce.R ) and a full-run console transcript ( reproduce.Rout ) against which every command can be checked. It also contains the precomputed Qwen3-Embedding-8B embeddings of the
auxiliary words (the five construct names and four projection poles)
and of the candidate items, together with the scripts that generated
them, the item embeddings from the two smaller models used in the
model-size comparison, the embeddings of the 42 items of the Depression
Anxiety Stress Scales from all three models, used in the Supplementary
Materials, and a script that re-embeds the items with each
model size and compares the result with the stored vectors. The 8B item embeddings themselves are bundled with the package. The item embeddings came from the Hugging Face revisions 97b0c614be4d77ee51c0cef4e5f07c00f9eb65b3 (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), 5cf2132abc99cad020ac570b19d031efec650f2b (4B), and 1d8ad4ca9b3dd8059ad90a75d4983776a23d44af (8B) of the model repositories ( qwen-2025 ) . Re-embedding the 50 items with these revisions, in single precision, without an instruction prompt, and on an NVIDIA H100 GPU, reproduced the stored vectors: the cosine between each new vector and the stored one was at least .999998 for every item and model size, and 1.000000 to six decimal places for the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales items. The output of this check is part of the archive. Results are stored as an .rds object and as CSV tables,
including the encoding comparison, the congruence matrix, both loading
matrices, the NLI similarity matrix, and the fits to random embeddings, alongside the regenerated
figures. The script documents where to download the human response file ( openpsychometrics-2018 ) and reads its location from an environment variable, so the archive does not depend on redistributing it. Two steps of the worked example call Python: reading the archived auxiliary and candidate-item embeddings from NumPy files, which uses the NumPy library ( harris-etal-2020 ) , and building the NLI matrix, which uses sentence-transformers ( reimers-gurevych-2019 ) and downloads its cross-encoder from the Hugging Face Hub on first run. All factor analyses, retention methods,
diagnostics, congruence metrics, refinement analyses, and figures are pure R
and run offline. The worked example was not preregistered.

blocks.en:
This section gives the technical detail behind the workflow described in
the main text. It has five parts. The Function Reference describes the
package’s functions for building, fitting, interpreting, and refining a
semantic factor solution, with the statistical rationale and source of
each. Retention Criteria and Monte Carlo Calibration then explain how
the package chooses the number of factors and how it judges model fit.
These are the two places where methods built for response data had to
be adapted to embedding similarity matrices. The Encoding Comparison
compares all the encodings on the agreement and fit metrics of the main
analysis. The last part explains the limits of the random-embedding
baselines that retention and calibration rely on, which is the main
problem the package leaves open.

blocks.en: Function Reference
blocks.zh: 函数参考

blocks.en:
Extraction and diagnostics. The main function, sfa() ,
runs the whole
workflow from raw item text, from precomputed embeddings, or from a
similarity matrix. It extracts factors by minimum residual through the
psych package ( revelle-2026 ) . Minimum residual chooses the loadings
so that the similarities the factors reproduce differ as little as
possible from the observed similarities. The function then rotates the
factors by oblimin. Oblimin is an oblique rotation, which allows the
factors to correlate, and it belongs to the family of analytic rotations
that includes varimax ( kaiser-1958 ) . Every fit reports the five
diagnostics that Table 1 in the main text defines:
the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy ( kaiser-1970 ) , printed with the descriptive labels of kaiser-rice-1974 , the root mean square residual (RMSR), the common
part accounted for (CAF) of lorenzo-seva-etal-2011 , the total
entropy fit index (TEFI) of golino-etal-2021 , and McDonald’s omega total for each factor ( revelle-zinbarg-2009 ) .
Omega is computed from one factor’s loadings λ i \lambda_{i} on a set of
items as ω = ( ∑ i λ i ) 2 / [ ( ∑ i λ i ) 2 + ∑ i ( 1 − λ i 2 ) ] \omega=(\sum_{i}\lambda_{i})^{2}/[(\sum_{i}\lambda_{i})^{2}+\sum_{i}(1-\lambda_{i}^{2})] . It is computed twice, once over the items whose
largest absolute loading is on the factor and once over the items of
the theoretical domain that the factor matches best, which is the domain
on whose items the factor’s mean absolute loading is largest. This is a
single-factor omega computed from the oblique pattern loadings, so it
ignores cross-loadings and differs from an omega for the full
five-factor model. Assignment by the largest absolute loading is also
arbitrary for items whose two largest loadings are nearly equal. When the
user supplies domain labels, sfa() also reports a matrix of average absolute loadings. Each entry of this
matrix is the mean absolute loading of one factor across the items of one
theoretical domain, and each factor is matched to the domain with its
largest entry. The matrix adapts the dominant average absolute loading
procedure that guenole-etal-2025 used to label factors. They
computed the averages over facets and added rules for factors that match
no domain or several, whereas the package computes them over items and
applies no such rules. The calibrate = TRUE option compares RMSR, CAF, and TEFI with their
values in fits to random embeddings (see Monte Carlo Calibration below).
The function as_psych() converts a fit into a psych::fa object, so
that the psych package’s own functions can be applied to it.
The function sfa_load_npz() reads embeddings that were
computed elsewhere and saved as NumPy .npz files, and it needs a
Python installation with the NumPy library. The function sfa_embed() embeds new text through Python with the
sentence-transformers library, and it downloads the chosen model on
first use.

blocks.en:
Similarity. The function sfa_similarity() turns a matrix of item
embeddings into an item-by-item similarity matrix. An encoding is the
rule it uses to do so, and the function offers four:
blocks.zh:
相似之处. 函数 sfa_simility () 转换项目矩阵
嵌入逐项相似性矩阵。 编码是
规则它使用它, 函数提供四:

blocks.en:
1. The atomic encoding takes the cosine similarity between the item
embeddings. guenole-etal-2025 applied this encoding and the next
to embeddings pooled over the items of each facet, and the package
applies them to single items. 2. The atomic_reversed encoding multiplies each reverse-keyed item’s
embedding by − 1 -1 before taking cosines ( guenole-etal-2025 ) . It is
the only encoding that needs the scoring key. 3. The squid encoding of pellert-etal-2026 , named for
Survey and Questionnaire Item Embeddings Differentials (SQuID), subtracts
the questionnaire embedding from every item’s embedding before taking
cosines. The questionnaire embedding is the mean of all the item
embeddings, and subtracting it can produce negative similarities between
items, which raw cosines rarely do ( pellert-etal-2026 ) . The
original method correlated the centered embeddings, whereas the package
takes cosines. 4. The mean_centered_pearson encoding, the default, subtracts each
embedding’s own mean value from all of its entries before taking
cosines. The cosine of two centered vectors equals their Pearson
correlation, so the result is a Pearson correlation matrix, which can
differ from the matrix of raw cosines ( pokropek-2026 ) .

blocks.en:
A fifth route uses no embeddings. The function sfa_nli_matrix() scores every ordered pair of items with a cross-encoder trained for
natural language inference (NLI), the task of judging whether one
sentence entails, contradicts, or is neutral toward another ( bowman-etal-2015 ) . A
model of this kind reads two sentences together and estimates the probabilities that the first
entails the second, that it contradicts the second, and that it does
neither. The score of an ordered pair is the probability of entailment
minus the probability of contradiction, a signed mapping in the spirit
of hommel-arslan-2025 , who gave contradicting pairs negative
similarities. Entailment is directional, so the two orders
of a pair can receive different scores, and the function averages them
to make the matrix symmetric. The resulting matrix need not be positive
semi-definite. A matrix that is not positive semi-definite has at least
one negative eigenvalue, so it cannot be the correlation matrix of any
set of variables. The function returns the matrix as it is. When a matrix with a negative
eigenvalue is passed to sfa() , sfa() prints a message and
replaces it with a positive-definite correlation matrix. It raises every eigenvalue below 10 − 6 10^{-6} to 10 − 6 10^{-6} , rebuilds the matrix from the adjusted
eigenvalues, and rescales it so that every diagonal entry is one.

blocks.en:
Interpretation. The function sfa_anchor() adapts the
approach of wulff-mata-2025 . It computes each item’s belonging to
each construct as the cosine similarity between the item’s raw embedding
and the construct’s anchor, so it does not use the similarity matrix that
was factored. Belonging is the semantic counterpart of a loading. An anchor is
either a construct’s centroid or its name embedding. The centroid is the
mean embedding of the construct’s items, and the name embedding is the
embedding of the construct’s name, such as extraversion . When the
function computes an item’s belonging to its own construct, it leaves
the item out of the centroid, so that the item is not compared with an
average that contains it. The printed output lists the eight items with
the lowest belonging to their own construct and marks each of them that
belongs more strongly to another construct.

The function sfa_project() adapts the semantic projection of grand-etal-2022 . It defines an axis as the difference between the
embeddings of two poles, such as calm minus anxious , where
a pole given as several words is the mean of their embeddings. Grand et
al. projected words onto lines defined by several pairs of opposite
words. The package instead scores each item by the cosine c c between its
embedding and the axis and then rescales the score as ( c − c low ) / ( c high − c low ) (c-c_{\mathrm{low}})/(c_{\mathrm{high}}-c_{\mathrm{low}}) , where c low c_{\mathrm{low}} and c high c_{\mathrm{high}} are the cosines of the two pole embeddings with the
axis. The low pole ( anxious ) therefore scores 0 and the high pole
( calm ) scores 1, and items can score outside that range.

blocks.en:
The function sfa_congruence() compares a fit with a theoretical assignment
of items to constructs, with a factor solution from responses, or with a
correlation matrix. It reports up to five metrics:
blocks.zh:
函数 sfa_congruence( ) 比较适配值和理论任务
,带有因子溶液,或
相关性矩阵。 它报告最多5个标准:

blocks.en:
1. Tucker’s congruence coefficient ϕ \phi for each pair of factors,
computed by psych::factor.congruence ( revelle-2026 ) , with
the benchmarks of lorenzo-seva-tenberge-2006 . It is
the cosine between the two factors’ columns of loadings, so it equals 1
when the two factors have the same pattern of loadings. 2. The normalized mutual information (NMI) between two assignments of
items to groups, which earlier embedding work also used to score
recovered structures ( garrido-etal-2025 ; golino-2026 ) . A factor
solution becomes an assignment by placing each item with the factor on
which its absolute loading is largest. NMI is the mutual information of
the two assignments divided by the geometric mean of their entropies ( strehl-ghosh-2002 ) . garrido-etal-2025 divided by the
arithmetic mean of the entropies instead, which gives similar but not
identical values. It is 0 when knowing
one assignment says nothing about the other and 1 when the two
assignments are identical. 3. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) of hubert-arabie-1985 between
the same two assignments. It counts the item pairs that both assignments
place together or both place apart, as a proportion of all pairs, and
corrects that proportion so that chance agreement scores 0 and identical
assignments score 1. 4. The Frobenius similarity between the factor-correlation matrices of
the two solutions. It is the cosine between the two matrices after each
is written out as a single list of numbers. The matrices are compared in
the order in which each solution reports its factors, without first
matching the factors, so the value depends on that order. It is
therefore not interpreted in this article. 5. The disattenuated item-pair correlation. It is the correlation
between the item-pair entries of the semantic matrix and those of the
comparison matrix, divided by the square root of the product of the two
matrices’ reliabilities. Each matrix’s reliability is estimated by splitting its item-pair entries
into odd- and even-numbered halves in the order in which the entries are
stored, correlating the halves, and stepping the result up with the
Spearman–Brown formula ( brown-1910 ; spearman-1910 ) . The division by
the reliabilities is the correction for attenuation of spearman-1904-proof . This split depends on the order of the items
and is not a standard reliability estimate. The result is capped at 1,
so a value of 1 can hide a larger uncorrected value. When either
reliability is not positive, the correction is undefined, and the metric
is reported as missing with a warning.

blocks.en:
The function sfa_jinglejangle() screens a set of scales for
jingle–jangle fallacies ( wulff-mata-2025 ; wulff-mata-2026 ) . A
jingle fallacy is giving the same name to scales that measure different things. A jangle fallacy is giving different names to scales that
measure the same thing. For every pair of scales, the function compares the cosine between the
embeddings of the two scales’ names with the cosine between the means of
their raw item embeddings. By default it flags the pair when the two similarities
differ by 0.20 or more. This single threshold is the package’s own. wulff-mata-2025 instead set separate cutoffs for the two
similarities from quantiles of their distributions.

测量相同的东西。 对于每对天平,函数将余弦比作

blocks.en:
Refinement. The function sfa_redundancy() flags pairs of items that
are locally dependent, which means that they share more than the factor
they both measure, typically because they say nearly the same thing. By
default it uses Unique Variable Analysis (UVA) as described by christensen-etal-2023 . UVA first estimates a network in which the
items are nodes and each link is the partial correlation between two
items, the correlation that remains when all other items are held
constant. The network is estimated with EBICglasso ( golino-christensen-2026 ) . EBICglasso is the graphical lasso ( friedman-etal-2008 ) , which sets
weak links to zero, with the strength of that penalty chosen by the
extended Bayesian information criterion ( foygel-drton-2010 ) . EBICglasso needs a sample size,
and a similarity matrix has none, so the package supplies a nominal
sample size of 1,000 or 20 times the number of items, whichever is
larger. This value is a fixed convention rather than an estimate. In the
worked example the number of flagged pairs was the same with 500 and
2,000, but for other scales the flagged pairs could change with it.
UVA then computes the weighted topological overlap (wTO) of every pair of
items. The wTO of two items is high when they are linked with similar
strengths to the same other items. Pairs whose absolute wTO is 0.25 or
more, the cutoff that christensen-etal-2023 recommend, are
flagged. From each redundant cluster the function keeps the item with
the highest mean absolute similarity to all the items and suggests
removing the others. A simpler alternative flags pairs whose absolute similarity in the
fitted matrix is 0.80 or more.

blocks.en:
The function sfa_simplify() builds a short form without responses ( jung-seo-2025 ; wang-etal-2026 ) . It offers two ways of choosing
items. The default, "anchor" , keeps in each construct the items
most similar to the construct’s centroid, with each item left out of the
centroid it is compared with. This is in the spirit of wang-etal-2026 , who selected the items with the highest
cluster-membership probability. The alternative, "medoid" , chooses
items within each construct one at a time, each time taking an item that
is close to the centroid and far from the items already chosen. It gives
up some closeness to the centroid in exchange for broader coverage of the
construct. The function then refits the shortened scale with the same encoding,
chooses its number of factors by parallel analysis, and compares it
with the full scale on the number of factors retained and on agreement
with the theoretical domains (NMI and ARI). It labels the result a
candidate that still needs validation with response data.

blocks.en:
The function sfa_item_fit() extends the anchoring approach of wulff-mata-2025 to newly written items. It embeds each candidate
item with the model recorded in the fit, or with another model or
embedding function that the user supplies. It then reports the
candidate’s cosine with each construct’s name embedding and with the
centroid of each construct’s raw item embeddings, the gap between the
construct it is most similar to and the next one, and its similarity to
the nearest existing item. A gap below 0.07 marks a cross-loader, and a
gap from 0.07 to 0.15 is reported as some cross-loading risk. The
candidate’s similarity to its best construct is called typical when it
lies within 0.05 of the average for that construct’s items, each item
compared with a centroid that leaves it out. A candidate whose
similarity to an existing item is 0.90 or more, the default cutoff, is
flagged as a near-duplicate. These cutoffs are heuristics of the
package, not published criteria.

blocks.en:
Display. The function sfa_corplot() draws the similarity matrix as
a heatmap with the items grouped by factor. The function sfa_itemplot() maps
the items to two dimensions by t t -distributed stochastic neighbor
embedding ( vandermaaten-hinton-2008 ) , computed with the Rtsne
package ( krijthe-2023 ) , uniform manifold
approximation and projection ( mcinnes-etal-2018 ) , computed with the
uwot package ( melville-2025 ) , principal component analysis, or classical multidimensional scaling. On these maps, items
with similar meanings appear close together. The plot() method
for a fit draws either a heatmap of the loadings or a scree plot of the
eigenvalues in decreasing order. The scree plot in the main text was
drawn directly from the eigenvalues of the similarity matrix, with the
parallel-analysis thresholds added.

blocks.en: Retention Criteria
blocks.zh: 保留标准

blocks.en:
Retention is the decision of how many factors to keep. Some retention
criteria compare the observed eigenvalues with the eigenvalues that
sampling error would produce in a sample of a given size. These criteria
cannot be applied to a similarity matrix unchanged, because a similarity
matrix comes from no sample. The package adapts them by putting random
embeddings of the same size as the real ones, or the embedding
dimension, where the sample would go. The function sfa_nfactors() reports the consensus of up to
five criteria, which is the number of factors chosen most often, with a
tie going to the smaller number. The criteria are not independent. With
its reference values floored at one, for example, the empirical Kaiser
criterion gave the same answer as the Kaiser rule on all three embedding
matrices analyzed here. The five criteria are the following:

这里分析的矩阵。 五项标准如下:

blocks.en:
1. Parallel analysis ( horn-1965 ) , computed by sfa_parallel() . Its comparison eigenvalues come from the
similarity matrices of random embeddings. Each random embedding is a set
of random vectors of unit length with the same number of items and the
same embedding dimension as the real embeddings. By default the function
builds 100 such matrices and compares each eigenvalue with the 95th
percentile of the corresponding random eigenvalues, rather than with the
mean that horn-1965 used. Following Horn, it counts the leading
eigenvalues that exceed their thresholds and stops at the first that does
not, so an eigenvalue that exceeds its threshold after that point is not
counted. 2. The Kaiser rule ( kaiser-1960 ) , which keeps every factor whose
eigenvalue is greater than one. The package applies it unchanged. 3. The empirical Kaiser criterion of braeken-vanassen-2017 ,
computed by sfa_ekc() with the embedding dimension n n in place
of the sample size. For J J items, each eigenvalue is compared with a
reference value. The reference value is ( 1 + J / n ) 2 (1+\sqrt{J/n})^{2} , which is
approximately the largest eigenvalue expected from n n observations of J J unrelated variables, multiplied by the average variance that remains
per eigenvalue once the earlier eigenvalues are subtracted from the
total. No reference value is allowed to fall below one. Factors are kept
up to the first eigenvalue that does not exceed its reference value. braeken-vanassen-2017 derived and evaluated the criterion for
correlation matrices of sample data, so its use with the embedding
dimension in place of the sample size goes beyond the conditions they
studied. 4. The TEFI criterion, which keeps the number of factors whose solution
has the lowest TEFI, the Von Neumann entropy version of the index ( golino-etal-2021 ) . golino-etal-2021 developed the index to
compare candidate structures of at least two factors with simple
structure. The package applies it unchanged to the similarity matrix,
fitting solutions with 1 to 15 factors by the extraction and rotation of
the main fit and keeping the number with the lowest TEFI. This scan over
the number of factors goes beyond the comparisons of candidate structures
that golino-etal-2021 tested. They also found that the index can
indicate too few factors when loadings and correlations between factors
are both high, although the problem seemed to vanish with more items per
factor. Their simulations used binary items and two or three factors with four
or eight items each, so the ten items per domain here lie outside the
conditions they studied. They also left the extension of the index to
one-factor structures to future work, so the one-factor candidate in the
package’s scan lies outside the structures the index was developed
for. On these matrices it chose two factors at
every model size, fewer than the theory contains. 5. Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA), run through the EGAnet package ( golino-christensen-2026 ) . EGA ( golino-epskamp-2017 ) estimates
a network of the items and keeps one factor for each community it
finds. A community is a group of
items more strongly linked to one another than to the other items. In
the benchmark of garrido-etal-2025 , which used personality items
written by a language model (GPT-4o) and a single embedding model, EGA
recovered the number of dimensions of embedding matrices more often than
parallel analysis and the Kaiser rule, both applied with principal
component extraction. That benchmark estimated its networks with
EBICglasso, which requires a sample size. The package instead uses the triangulated maximally filtered graph ( massara-etal-2016 ) , which builds the network from the similarity
matrix alone, and it finds communities with the Walktrap algorithm ( pons-latapy-2006 ) .

blocks.en:
Two further tools were not part of the consensus. Velicer’s minimum
average partial test ( velicer-1976 ) , computed by sfa_map() , removes the first m m principal components from the matrix for
increasing values of m m , up to two fewer than the number of items, and
keeps the m m at which the average squared partial correlation among the
items is smallest. On the present matrix it indicated removing 10
components, well beyond the five domains the
inventory was written to measure. Including it would have added a vote

blocks.en:
The function sfa_dimselect() addresses a question that only embeddings
raise, which is how many of an embedding’s coordinates are needed to
recover the structure. It adapts the embedding-depth optimization of golino-2026 , using
ordinary EGA on the leading coordinates where Golino used dynamic EGA.
For a grid of 148 depths d d , it rebuilds the
similarity matrix from the first d d coordinates of each embedding, in
their stored order, and runs EGA with the triangulated maximally
filtered graph and the Walktrap algorithm. The grid has 147
depths spaced 28 apart, from 3 to
4,091 leading coordinates, plus the full embedding of
4,096 coordinates. The function then rescales two quantities across the depths so that each
runs from 0 at its lowest value to 1 at its highest. These are the NMI
between the EGA communities and the theoretical domains, and the TEFI of
the EGA solution. The chosen depth maximizes 0.70 × NMI − 0.30 × TEFI 0.70\times\mathrm{NMI}-0.30\times\mathrm{TEFI} computed on the rescaled values, so the
weights favor agreement with the theoretical domains over entropy fit:

blocks.en: Monte Carlo Calibration
blocks.zh: 蒙特卡洛校准

blocks.en:
Conventional cutoffs for fit statistics, such as a standardized root
mean square residual of about .08 or below ( hu-bentler-1999 ) , were
derived from fits to simulated samples of respondents, so they were set
with the sampling error of correlations in mind. An embedding similarity
matrix has no respondents. The values its fit statistics take by chance
depend instead on the items and the embedding space, so cutoffs such as
the one for the standardized root mean square residual can be too lenient
for it, as pokropek-2026 found for confirmatory models with few
indicators. In his simulations the share of random models that passed
the standardized root mean square residual cutoff fell from 95% with
four indicators to 66% with eight, and he judged the cutoffs for the
comparative fit index, the Tucker–Lewis index, and the root mean square
error of approximation appropriate with six or more indicators. Many model-based tests and indexes of fit
require a sample size, which a similarity matrix lacks ( suarez-alvarez-etal-2026 ) . The calibrate = TRUE option
supplies a reference. With a fixed seed (42 by default), it draws sets of
vectors from a standard normal distribution, with the same number of
items and the same embedding dimension as the scale, and rescales each
vector to unit length. Such vectors share no semantic structure by
construction. The function takes the raw cosines among each set,
whatever encoding the real fit used, so the random vectors are not
centered, whereas the default encoding of the observed fit centers each
embedding. It fits the same number of factors
with the same extraction and rotation, and records the values of RMSR,
CAF, and TEFI. A replicate whose fit fails is dropped, and in the worked example
100 of 100 replicates were retained. Their values are written
to output/calibration_null.csv in the reproduction archive. The transcript reports 20 warnings that the oblimin
rotation stopped at its limit of 1,000 iterations without converging,
and a single fit can issue this warning many times. Rerunning the
replicates with the same random draws, which reproduced their RMSR
values exactly, and counting the warnings fit by fit showed that all
20 came from one fit, so the rotation
failed to converge in one of the 100 fits. RMSR and CAF do not depend on the rotation, but TEFI,
which uses each item’s assignment to a factor, does. The remaining
warning repeats that the keying-free encoding ignores the scoring
column. This procedure
adapts the reference distributions of pokropek-2026 , which were
built from words drawn at random from the same text corpus as the real
words. Words drawn this way keep the general thematic similarity that
real words share, whereas random unit vectors do not.

blocks.en:
Across the random replicates, RMSR ranged from .0119 to
.0134 (mean .0127), CAF from .501 to
.532 (mean .507, S ​ D = .003 SD=.003 ), and TEFI from − 21.66 -21.66 to − 17.82 -17.82 (mean − 20.85 -20.85 , S ​ D = 0.53 SD=0.53 ). Over the 99 replicates whose rotation
converged, TEFI ranged from − 21.66 -21.66 to − 18.80 -18.80 . Each statistic needs its own
reading. The random fits passed the conventional RMSR cutoff easily,
because the cosines among random unit vectors are close to zero and
leave the factors almost nothing to reproduce. RMSR grows with the size
of the similarities being reproduced, so the observed RMSR (.032),
although above the whole random range, cannot be read as misfit, and
passing the cutoff says little about fit. The observed TEFI ( − 27.71 -27.71 ) was lower than every random value, so
none of the 100 random fits was as low, which shows only that
the real items are not random. CAF is about .5 when the residuals share
no structure, as in the random fits, and the observed CAF (.412) was
lower than every random value. This suggests that the similarities the
five factors leave unexplained still share structure that random
embeddings lack, although, as for RMSR, a baseline of near-zero
similarities makes this a weak contrast. These results echo the finding of pokropek-2026 that, for
confirmatory models with few indicators and for the standardized root
mean square residual, values produced by chance can pass conventional
thresholds. We therefore recommend reporting calibrated values alongside
the conventional ones, with the caveat that the random-embedding baseline
is weak. Which baseline to calibrate against is still the
analyst’s choice, as discussed under Limits of the Random-Embedding
Baselines below.

blocks.en:
Three patterns appear in Table S1 . First, atomic_reversed agreed least of the four embedding encodings
with the correlations among reverse-scored responses ( r keyed = .137 r_{\text{keyed}}=.137 , against
.434 for atomic , the same encoding without the sign
flip), and its agreement with the raw correlations ( r raw = .444 r_{\text{raw}}=.444 ) was close to that of atomic and mean_centered_pearson .
Reverse-scoring a response keeps its content and inverts only the rating
scale. Multiplying an embedding by − 1 -1 , by contrast, reverses the whole vector,
which plausibly makes it point away from the item’s topic as well as
from its position on the trait. In the similarity matrix the flip only
changes the signs of some entries, so it cannot change the grouping of
the items, and the NMI, ARI, KMO, RMSR, and CAF of atomic_reversed equal those of atomic by construction.
Its lower agreement with the reverse-scored correlations likely reflects
the signs it imposes. Every unflipped cosine is positive, so the flip makes
the similarity of every forward-keyed item with every reverse-keyed item
negative, whereas reverse-scoring is meant to make the items of a domain
correlate positively whatever their keying. The flip is compared with the
reverse-scored correlations because it applies the same scoring key, and
against the raw responses it gave no gain. The sign flip also makes the split-half reliability of the
similarity matrix negative, so the disattenuated correlation is
undefined. The package reports that value as missing, with a warning that
names the cause, rather than dropping it from the output.

blocks.en: Limits of the Random-Embedding Baselines
blocks.zh: 随机编辑基线的限度

blocks.en:
Both the adapted parallel analysis and the fit calibration compare the
real similarity matrix with matrices built from random unit vectors. In
thousands of dimensions such vectors are nearly orthogonal, which means
that the cosine between any two of them is close to 0. Their similarity matrix is therefore close to an identity matrix, and
the parallel-analysis thresholds derived from it lie near one. For the
8B embeddings the first threshold was 1.23, and the thresholds
declined across eigenvalue positions to 1.14 at the
eighth. These random vectors are not centered, whereas the observed
matrix of the default encoding is. Real item embeddings, by contrast,
are positively similar to one another in the worked example, as
hidden-state representations from contextual language models commonly
are ( ethayarajh-2019 ) , so
their similarity
matrix has one very large eigenvalue that reflects this shared
similarity. Exceeding the random-embedding baseline, built from nearly
unrelated vectors, is a weak test for such a matrix. In practice the adapted parallel analysis behaves like a Kaiser rule
with a cutoff a little above one that declines slowly across eigenvalue
positions, which makes it somewhat stricter than the Kaiser rule here
(first thresholds 1.50, 1.31, and 1.23
for the three model sizes). Its verdict therefore shows which
eigenvalues exceed that cutoff rather than where interpretable structure
ends.

blocks.en:
A better choice of random vectors would not remove the problem.
Conventional retention baselines model what sampling respondents does to
a correlation matrix when no factors are present. An embedding
similarity matrix, by contrast, is fully determined by the items and the
embedding model, and nothing was sampled to produce it. Any baseline for
such a matrix must therefore stipulate what varies from one draw to the
next, a decision that a sampling design would otherwise make. The
baseline of pokropek-2026 , built from words drawn at random from
a text corpus, keeps the general thematic similarity that real items
share, which random unit vectors lack. Two other alternatives both indicate too many factors, for different
reasons. Parallel analysis with simulated-data comparison matrices
indicated too many factors on embedding matrices in the benchmark of garrido-etal-2025 . With comparison
data generated from factor models, the reproduction of the observed
eigenvalues improves with every added factor. Presumably, a factor model with one unique variance per item cannot
reproduce the many small eigenvalues of an embedding similarity matrix,
which decline gradually, so each added comparison factor captures more
of them (see Comparison-Data Misfit
Profiles below). The
same procedure applied to the human responses shows a sharp elbow at
exactly five factors. The eigenvalues of embedding similarity matrices
therefore appear to decline with no sharp boundary between major and
minor factors. If so, a single number of factors for such a matrix
records how much minor structure the analyst chose to keep, not a
boundary in the data.

blocks.en:
A retention test suited to embedding similarity matrices would need
reference data generated from item embeddings themselves. These would be
sets of items whose factor structure is known in advance and whose
embeddings have the geometry of real ones. Such a benchmark could also
train and validate a machine-learning criterion in the spirit of the
comparison data forest ( goretzko-ruscio-2024 ) . Until such a
benchmark exists, we recommend reporting retention on embedding
similarity matrices as the consensus of several criteria together with
the comparison-data misfit profile, and checking agreement with theory
across several candidate numbers of factors.

blocks.en:
The comparison-data method of ruscio-roche-2012 treats retention
as a comparison between models rather than as a test against a baseline
with no structure. For each candidate number of factors k k , it asks how
well data generated to have exactly k k factors reproduce the observed
eigenvalues. The method has four steps:
blocks.zh:
Ruscio-roche-2012的比较数据方法处理保留问题
作为模型之间的比较,而不是对基准的试验
没有结构。 对于每个候选系数Kk,它询问如何
生成良好的数据,以精确地复制观测到的 k 系数
精华. 该方法有四个步骤:

blocks.en:
1. For each k k , generate a large population of comparison data whose
correlations follow the k k -factor model fitted to the observed
correlations and whose variables have the observed distributions. 2. Draw random samples from that population, each the same size as
the observed data. 3. For each sample, compute the root mean square difference between
its eigenvalues and the observed eigenvalues. This difference is the
misfit of k k factors, and it is small when k k factors account for the
observed eigenvalues well. 4. Compare the misfits of successive values of k k .

blocks.en:
Because each candidate number of factors is judged against the
one before it, the method does not need a baseline with no structure,
which is the weak point of the adapted parallel analysis (see Limits of
the Random-Embedding Baselines above). The comparison populations are generated with an adaptation of the GenData algorithm of ruscio-kaczetow-2008 . GenData draws each variable from its target
distribution and iteratively adjusts an intermediate correlation matrix
so that the generated data reproduce the target correlations as closely
as possible. It stops when several adjustments in a row bring no
improvement. The adaptation in sfa_cd() instead makes a fixed
sequence of six adjustments and keeps the population that reproduced the
target correlations best.

respondents play in response data. This is a heuristic, because the
dimensions are not sampled like respondents, and the resulting numbers of cases (1,024 to 4,096) exceed the range of
sample sizes, 200 to 1,000, for which the method was validated ( ruscio-roche-2012 ) . The Pearson correlations between
items computed across the embedding dimensions equal the mean_centered_pearson similarities, so the profile describes

For the human responses, the relative improvement rose with each added
factor up to the fifth, which reduced the misfit by

of the Big Five responses therefore show a sharp boundary after the
fifth factor, which is where the theory places it. This profile comes
from one random subsample of 2,500 respondents, although the
elbow is large enough that another draw is unlikely to remove it. The three embedding
matrices showed no such elbow. Each added factor reduced their misfit by between 9% and
22%, with no spike comparable to the human one at any

remained at five factors. Presumably, a factor model with one unique
variance per item cannot reproduce the many small eigenvalues of an embedding
similarity matrix, which decline gradually, so each added comparison
factor keeps improving the reproduction.

The human responses show how the rule behaves on response data. Besides
the subsample of 2,500 respondents behind the profile, we drew
subsamples of 250, 500, and 1,000 respondents. All four were drawn after
the same seed, 42, so each smaller subsample is the first part of the
larger ones, and the four are nested. Five further subsamples of 250 and
of 500 respondents were drawn with the seeds 1 to 5, and with each of
these seeds, too, the subsample of 250 is the first part of the
subsample of 500. These seeds governed only the choice of respondents,
because the random steps inside sfa_cd() used the seed 42 in
every run. In the subsample of 250 drawn with the seed 42, near the lower
end of the sample sizes for which the method was validated, the rule
stopped at seven factors, and the five further

eight to ten. The sequential rule therefore did

consistent with the ten factors that conventional

respondents (see Retention Criteria above), although the cap prevents a

blocks.en:
These results are consistent with an account based on statistical
power. On this account, the test detects smaller reductions in misfit
as the number of cases grows, so with enough respondents the rule keeps adding factors
beyond the five interpretable ones. The embedding matrices, with 1,024
to 4,096 dimensions as cases, may reach the cap for the same reason
rather than because of a property peculiar to embeddings. The results do
not establish this account. The test’s p p values also depend on the 500
simulated samples for each number of factors, and the embedding
dimensions only play the role of cases, so the comparison with the human
subsamples is an analogy. On the embedding matrices, moreover, the
profiles show no boundary for the rule to detect. Taken together, the profiles support the
practice recommended in the main text, which is to report retention as
the consensus of several criteria and to check agreement with theory
across several candidate numbers of factors.

blocks.en:
In the main text, the separation between the Big Five domains did not
rise steadily from the 0.6B to the 8B model. Because that comparison
used a single inventory, it was repeated with a second one, the
Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS). The DASS has 42 items, 14 for
each of three scales, and each item describes a negative emotional
symptom, such as “I found myself getting upset by quite trivial
things” ( lovibond-lovibond-1995 ) . The scale’s history makes it a useful second case. Its Stress
scale grew out of items that did not separate anxiety from depression,
and in its authors’ factor analysis of responses, the Anxiety and Stress
factors merged into one when only two factors were extracted ( lovibond-lovibond-1995 ) .

”(1995年) 规模的历史使它成为有用的第二个案例。 它的压力

The 42 items were embedded with the same three models and the same
settings as the Big Five items. Re-embedding them with the model
revisions given in the Open Practices Statement reproduced the stored
vectors, with a cosine of 1.000000 to six decimal places
between each new vector and the stored one. The comparison then used the
statistics of the main text. The first is the point-biserial correlation
between sharing a scale and a pair’s similarity, over all
861 item pairs, with an item-level bootstrap 95% interval.
The second is the gap between the mean similarity of pairs within a
scale and that of pairs between scales. Because the same resampled items
served all three sizes, the bootstrap also gave an interval for the
difference between two sizes. Finally, three factors were extracted at
each size, the theoretical number, and each item was assigned to the
factor on which it loaded most strongly. The agreement of this
assignment with the three scales was measured with the normalized mutual
information (NMI) and the adjusted Rand index (ARI), as in the main text,
and compared with a permutation baseline, the largest values reached
when the item assignment of the 8B solution was compared with 1,000
random permutations of the scale labels. For comparison,
Table S4 also gives the same agreement for the
five-factor Big Five solution at each size.

(Table S4 ). With the Big Five it stayed nearly
constant. The paired 95% interval for the DASS increase from 0.6B to 8B
ran from − .001 -.001 to .053, so it only just
included zero, whereas the Big Five interval for the same increase ran
from − .012 -.012 to .013. The point-biserial
correlation rose only slightly, from .481 to
.505 and .510, and its intervals overlapped
widely. The three scales did not change alike
(Figure S4 ). The gaps of Depression (.118,
.129, and .180) and Stress
(.126, .144, and .158)
grew with size, whereas the gap of Anxiety shrank (.053,
.044, and .034).

blocks.en:
The clearest change was in the three-factor solutions. Under the 0.6B
model, the factor with the most Anxiety items (eight
of 14) also took all 14 Stress items, so
most Anxiety items and the Stress items formed a single factor, as
Anxiety and Stress did in the two-factor solution of responses that lovibond-lovibond-1995 reported.
Under the 8B model, each scale had a factor of its own, and these
factors took 14 Depression, 14
Stress, and 11 Anxiety items, out of 14 each. Agreement with the
three scales rose accordingly, from NMI = .412 and
ARI = .271 for 0.6B to .700 and
.650 for 4B and .834 and
.801 for 8B, all above the largest values reached with
permuted labels (.249 and .195). With the Big
Five, agreement did not rise with size. It was highest for 4B
(NMI = .693, ARI = .574), against
.497 and .393 for 0.6B and .527
and .402 for 8B. Neither parallel analysis nor the
consensus of the five retention criteria indicated three factors for the
DASS at any size. Parallel analysis retained
four factors at every size, and the consensus of the
five criteria was five for 0.6B,
four for 4B, and four for 8B.

blocks.en:
The 0.6B solution was not the only one. psych ( revelle-2026 ) starts the oblique rotation from several
orientations, most of them random, and keeps the result with the largest
share of loadings close to zero, which is not necessarily the one with
the lowest value of the rotation criterion. The seed argument of sfa() does not set these random orientations, so the
reproduction script sets the random seed before each DASS fit. To see how
far the results depend on the orientations drawn, each three-factor DASS
fit and each five-factor Big Five fit was repeated under
40 random seeds. Judged by their agreement with the scales,
every fit but one gave the same solution under every seed. The exception was the 0.6B DASS fit, which gave the
solution reported here under 16 seeds and a second
solution under the other 24. In the second solution,
all 14 Anxiety items and 13 of the
14 Stress items loaded most strongly on one factor, and agreement with the scales
was higher (NMI = .665, ARI = .514), although still
lower than for 4B. The reported solution had the lower value of the
oblimin criterion, which the rotation minimizes (0.564
against 0.567). Two of the refits ended with a warning that the
rotation had not converged, and neither gave a solution other than those
described here. Neither solution separated Anxiety from
Stress.

blocks.en:
The DASS thus showed a clearer effect of model size than the Big Five.
The smallest model merged two scales that are also closely related in
responses, and the largest separated all three. The two inventories
differ in many ways besides the effect of size, including the number of
scales and the kind of content their items describe, so two inventories
cannot show which of these properties makes model size matter.
